title: Article og:image carries no width/height and no article:author, article:tag or article:section is emitted
why:
REFUTED on three grounds: a fabricated citation, an SEO-folklore core claim, and a residual issue that is not an organic-search issue at all.

1. FABRICATED EVIDENCE. The finding states imgWidth/imgHeight "are already destructured into frontMatter at :96-97". They are not. Verified verbatim, app/blog/[...slug]/page.js:90-99 is:
```
  const frontMatter = {
    slug: slugStr,
    date: article.date,
    title: article.title,
    tags: article.tags,
    lastmod: article.lastmod,
    summary: article.summary,     // line 96
    images: article.images,       // line 97
    readingTime: readingTime(article.content),
  }
```
Lines 96-97 are summary and images. A repo-wide grep for imgWidth|imgHeight returns zero hits in app/blog/[...slug]/page.js. The claimed variable is not in scope where the finding says it is.

2. THE CORPUS CLAIM IS UNVERIFIABLE AND LIKELY WRONG. "77 of 77 published articles" have imgWidth/imgHeight cannot be checked: data/blog is empty (0 files) and no local article index exists. The code contradicts the assumption of universal population: lib/articles.js:133-134 `imgWidth: data.imgWidth || null, imgHeight: data.imgHeight || null` and scripts/migrate-blog-to-s3.js:440-441 (identical) make null a supported stored value, and components/admin/ArticleMetadataForm.js:341-342 explicitly writes null back. The proposed fix would therefore emit `width: null, height: null` into openGraph.images for any such article. components/articles/ArticleItem.js:10 already guards with `imgWidth && imgHeight &&` precisely because they can be absent, which is the repo's own evidence against 77/77.

3. THE RANKING CLAIM IS FOLKLORE AND IS ALREADY HANDLED. Open Graph `article:author`, `article:tag` and `article:section` are Facebook namespace tags. Google does not use them as ranking or E-E-A-T signals. The authorship signal Google actually documents is schema.org Article `author`, and the page ALREADY emits it: app/blog/[...slug]/page.js:111-114 `author: authorDetails.map((author) => ({ '@type': 'Person', name: author.name }))` inside the JSON-LD injected at :127-130. The topical signal is likewise already present as crawlable linked content at BlogPost.js:103-113 (`tags.map((tag) => <Tag key={tag} text={tag} />)`). Per the ground rule "do not report a problem the code already handles somewhere else", this half is refuted twice over.

4. THE RESIDUAL IS NOT SEO. What survives verification is only that openGraph.images at :42 (and twitter.images at :48) pass bare strings, so no og:image:width/height/alt is emitted. That is confirmed: no opengraph-image.js exists under app/ (find returns nothing), so Next.js's file-convention auto-dimensions do not apply, and Next does not infer dimensions for string URLs. But this affects Facebook/WhatsApp first-scrape card rendering only. It has zero effect on organic search ranking or indexing of the articles, which is the stated priority of this audit. metadataBase is correctly set at app/layout.js:8, so the URLs themselves resolve.

Net: strip the fabricated line reference, the unverifiable 77/77, and the folklore, and nothing of SEO consequence remains. At most this is a low-severity social-card polish item, not a medium metadata defect. (Note for the parent: the genuine defect on this same line range is at :41, `url: ${siteMetadata.siteUrl}/blog/${slugStr}` producing a double slash because siteUrl ends in "/" — that belongs to the canonical/URL dimension, not to this finding.)

title: Article JSON-LD publisher logo is a relative path, which is invalid in structured data
why:
The code exists as quoted, but the SEO claim rests on obsolete Google guidance, and the proposed fix contains a false statement.

1) Code check (accurate). app/blog/[...slug]/page.js:115-122 does contain `publisher: { '@type': 'Organization', name: siteMetadata.author, logo: { '@type': 'ImageObject', url: siteMetadata.siteLogoLight } }`, and data/siteMetadata.js:11 is `siteLogoLight: '/static/images/sac-main-logo.png'`. Line 129 is `JSON.stringify(jsonLd)`. app/layout.js:8 sets `metadataBase: new URL(siteMetadata.siteUrl)`, which applies only to the Next.js Metadata API and does not touch the hand-serialised JSON-LD. So the value does render relative. That part is real.

2) The SEO impact claim is wrong. Google's current Article structured data documentation states: "There are no required properties; instead, add the properties that apply to your content." The recommended list is author, author.name, author.url, dateModified, datePublished, headline, image. `publisher` and `publisher.logo` are neither required nor recommended. The claim that "Google's Article rich-result parser requires an absolute publisher.logo URL" repeats the pre-2021 AMP-era requirement that Google removed.

3) The mechanism is wrong. The publisher logo in Search, knowledge panels, and attribution comes from Organization `logo` markup, not from Article `publisher.logo` (Google Search Central, "Expanding markup support for Organization details, including Logo structured data", Nov 2023). Google also states that no markup is required for Top Stories eligibility. An invalid Article publisher.logo cannot suppress a Discover or Top Stories logo.

4) The relative URL is not even malformed. The schema.org JSON-LD context types URL-valued properties as `@id`, and JSON-LD resolves relative IRIs against the document base IRI. On https://sac-website.vercel.app/blog/<slug> the value resolves to the correct absolute image URL.

5) The proposed fix contains a verifiably false claim. It says "Delete components/SEO.js ... grep confirms nothing imports them." pages/gallery.js:2 has `import { PageSEO } from '@/components/SEO'`, so SEO.js is live code. The `.../undefined` sub-bug at components/SEO.js:120 is real text, but it sits inside `BlogSEO`, which is imported only by layouts/PostLayout.js:4 and layouts/PostSimple.js:4. Nothing imports those two layouts, so that string never reaches a rendered page and has zero SEO impact.

A different, unclaimed gap is real: grep for `ld+json` finds only two blocks in the repo (app/blog/[...slug]/page.js:128 and the dead components/SEO.js:142). The site publishes no Organization or Logo structured data at all, which is the markup Google actually uses for the publisher logo. That is a separate finding, not this one.

Severity: low polish at most. Making the URL absolute is tidy, but it changes no rich-result eligibility.

title: The legacy pages/_document.js declares lang="en" on /gallery and the catch-all 404
why:
Half the evidence is wrong and the surviving half rests on obsolete SEO advice.

1) FABRICATED 404 CLAIM. The finding asserts "the unmatched-route 404 at /no-such-page also renders lang=en". That is false in this codebase. node_modules/next/dist/server/base-server.js:1683-1697 shows Next 16 resolving the App Router not-found entry FIRST whenever the app directory is enabled: `if (is404) { if (hasAppDir) { result = await this.findPageComponents({ ... page: _constants.UNDERSCORE_NOT_FOUND_ROUTE_ENTRY, isAppPath: true ... }); using404Page = result !== null; } if (!result && await this.hasPage('/404')) {`. The App Router always supplies a built-in default not-found (the "This page could not be found" markup lives in node_modules/next/dist/build/templates/app-page.js), so `result` is never null and pages/404.js is never reached. pages/404.js is dead code. An unmatched route renders inside app/layout.js and therefore emits lang="es". The claimed missing title/description/robots on the live 404 is likewise moot, and a page returning HTTP 404 is not indexed anyway, so it cannot "produce an ugly untitled entry".

2) OBSOLETE SEO REASONING. The stated impact, "Google uses lang to target Spanish-language results", contradicts Google's own multi-regional and multilingual documentation, which says Google uses only the visible content of the page to determine language and does not use code-level language information such as lang attributes. A wrong lang attribute costs nothing in Google ranking or language targeting. The genuine cost is accessibility (screen-reader pronunciation) and browser translate prompts. That is an a11y item, not an SEO item.

3) IMPACT OVERSTATED EVEN ON ITS OWN TERMS. pages/gallery.js has no getStaticProps and no getServerSideProps; the photos are fetched client-side in useEffect from /api/photos. None of the astrophotography is in the crawlable HTML, so the "page of Puerto Rico astrophotography with real ranking potential" premise does not apply to the served markup. The page is also not metadata-starved: pages/gallery.js:290 renders <PageSEO title="Galeria" description="Galeria de imagenes" />, and components/SEO.js:9-11 emits <title>, <meta name="robots" content="follow, index"> and the description.

4) DUPLICATE HEAD BLOCK IS NOT AN SEO ISSUE. pages/_document.js:7-28 and app/layout.js:47-58 belong to two different routers and never render on the same response. It is source duplication, not duplicated output. The missing Open+Sans in the pages-router font URL is a visual regression on /gallery, not a search issue.

What is literally true and survives: pages/_document.js:5 really is <Html lang="en">, app/layout.js:45 really is <html lang="es" suppressHydrationWarning>, there is no app/gallery route, and there is no mitigation anywhere (only those two lang= occurrences exist across app/, components/, pages/, lib/; no middleware.*, no vercel.json, no i18n block in next.config.js). So exactly one client-rendered page declares the wrong language. That is a low-severity accessibility and code-hygiene defect, not a medium SEO defect, and it touches no blog article route, which the brief prioritizes. The proposed migration is reasonable housekeeping but should not be justified as an SEO fix.

title: site.webmanifest has empty name fields, 404 icon paths, and a theme_color that contradicts the meta tag
why:
REFUTED as an SEO finding. The quoted code is accurate and no mitigation exists, but none of it affects organic search.

1) Google Search does not parse the web app manifest. name, short_name, manifest icons, and theme_color are PWA install metadata. They are not indexing, ranking, or SERP-appearance inputs. The audit brief prioritizes blog-article organic search, and this touches none of it.

2) The Lighthouse justification is obsolete. Lighthouse removed the PWA category entirely in v12 (2024), so there is no PWA audit left to fail. Manifest validity was never part of the Best Practices category either. The finding rests on outdated tooling advice.

3) The /favicon.ico claim is technically wrong. Google's root /favicon.ico fallback applies only when a page declares no icon link. app/layout.js:47-49 declare apple-touch-icon, favicon-32x32.png and favicon-16x16.png, and all three files exist in public/static/favicons/. Google uses the declared links, so no SERP favicon path is lost. SERP favicons are also a CTR nicety, never a ranking factor.

4) The theme-color "conflict" is not a conflict and is not non-deterministic. The meta tag at app/layout.js:52 governs browser chrome while browsing; the manifest theme_color governs an installed PWA. Different contexts, deterministic in each, zero search impact.

5) Severity is inflated. The real-world effect is a blank name and a missing icon in an Android "Add to home screen" prompt, which is cosmetic PWA polish, not a medium SEO defect. It belongs on a housekeeping list, not in an SEO audit. The proposed fix is harmless and cheap, but it will not move a single article's ranking, impressions, or indexability.

title: The legacy SEO component emits twitter:site as a full URL instead of an @handle
why:
The code evidence is 100% accurate (I confirmed every line verbatim), and no mitigation exists anywhere in the repo. I refute it on ground 3: this is not an SEO problem, and the stated impact rests on X card behavior that no longer exists.

1) Evidence check - all confirmed, nothing fabricated. components/SEO.js:23 is exactly `<meta name="twitter:site" content={siteMetadata.twitter} />`. data/siteMetadata.js:23 is exactly `twitter: 'https://twitter.com/soc_astrocaribe',`. app/layout.js:25 is exactly `site: '@soc_astrocaribe',`. Line numbers are all correct.

2) Mitigation check - none. `grep -rn "twitter:site|soc_astrocaribe"` across the repo returns exactly three hits: app/layout.js:25, components/SEO.js:23, data/siteMetadata.js:23. pages/_document.js and pages/_app.js set no twitter meta. There is no app/gallery route (`ls app` shows no gallery dir), so pages/gallery.js:290 `<PageSEO title="Galería" description="Galería de imágenes" />` is the live /gallery and the App Router root metadata does not reach it. The scope claim is correct.

3) Not an SEO defect - the refutation. No search engine consumes `twitter:*` markup. Google, Bing, and the rest read Open Graph and JSON-LD, never Twitter Card tags. This value cannot affect indexing, ranking, crawl, or SERP presentation on any page. The audit's own ground rule is to prioritize what hurts organic search for blog ARTICLES; this is a social-attribution tag on /gallery, which is not an article at all.

4) The claimed social impact is also wrong on the specifics. `twitter:site` is an OPTIONAL attribution field in X's card spec, not a card prerequisite. A malformed value is ignored; it does not suppress the card. The card on /gallery still renders from the sibling tags at components/SEO.js:22 (`twitter:card` = summary_large_image), :24 (`twitter:title`), :25 (`twitter:description`), and :26 (`twitter:image`). Beyond that, X's post-2023 link-card redesign stopped rendering the "via @handle" attribution line entirely (it strips even title and description text from timeline cards), so the "loses its site attribution" harm has no surface left to appear on. The finding's impact sentence describes card behavior that has not existed for years.

5) Severity was honestly rated (the author said low, not inflated), so there is nothing to downgrade. But "low = polish" still implies a real if minor SEO gain, and here the SEO gain is exactly zero. This is a code-consistency nit, not an SEO item.

6) One scope imprecision worth passing back: the proposed fix says deleting components/SEO.js is safe once gallery migrates. Three other files import it - layouts/AuthorLayout.js:3, layouts/PostLayout.js:4, layouts/PostSimple.js:4 - though I confirmed by grep that nothing imports those three layouts, so they are dead code. The deletion would need to remove them too.

Recommendation: drop from the SEO audit. If the team wants it, file it as a one-line code-tidiness item, not an SEO finding.

title: app/layout.js hand-writes a viewport meta that Next already injects
why:
Partly fabricated evidence, and the surviving part is not an SEO problem.

WHAT IS TRUE: app/layout.js:59 does contain `<meta content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1" name="viewport" />`, and Next 16.2.3 does emit its own copy (node_modules/next/dist/lib/metadata/default-metadata.js:23-27 `createDefaultViewport()` returns `width: 'device-width', initialScale: 1`; node_modules/next/dist/lib/metadata/metadata.js:245 pushes `name: "viewport"`). No `export const viewport` exists anywhere in the repo, so the default is never suppressed. The built article HTML confirms two tags.

WHAT IS FALSE: "pages/_app.js:26 adds a third copy for the pages-router routes." I checked the actual build output. `.next/server/pages/gallery.html` and `.next/server/pages/404.html` each contain EXACTLY ONE viewport meta. next/head's `unique()` filter (node_modules/next/dist/shared/lib/head.js:71-119) dedupes `<meta>` by its `name` category, so the explicit tag in _app.js replaces defaultHead()'s copy instead of adding to it. Separately, pages-router routes render a wholly separate document and never share a head with App Router routes, so "a third copy" is incoherent regardless. One third of the cited evidence is wrong.

WHY THE REMAINDER IS NOT AN SEO FINDING: both App Router tags carry byte-identical content (`width=device-width, initial-scale=1`). Google reads the first viewport declaration; Lighthouse's viewport audit passes; mobile-friendly evaluation passes. There is no crawling, indexing, ranking, or CTR consequence for the S3-backed blog articles this audit was told to prioritize. The claimed impact ("flagged by HTML validators and some SEO crawlers as a duplicate-tag warning") is asserted with no verification and is not correct as stated: HTML permits repeated `meta name=viewport`; only a small set of meta names (description, application-name) carry a uniqueness constraint, and mainstream crawlers (Screaming Frog, Ahrefs, Semrush) audit viewport for presence and configuration, not for duplication. The secondary rationale ("signals that the head is hand-managed, which is how the canonical and og gaps arose") is commentary about OTHER findings; those must stand on their own evidence and cannot lend severity to this one.

VERDICT: the code duplication is real but is a code-hygiene item, not an SEO defect. It does not belong in an SEO audit scored on indexability and ranking. The proposed fix (delete app/layout.js:59, add `export const viewport`) is harmless and reasonable as cleanup, but the pages/_app.js:25-27 half of it should be dropped from the rationale since no duplicate exists there. Note the fix's theme-color remark is also not a duplication issue: `createDefaultViewport()` returns `themeColor: null`, so Next emits nothing that collides with app/layout.js:51-52.

title: With no sitemap, article discovery depends entirely on a Prev/Next-only chain 16 pages deep
why:
The quoted code is real, but the central claim is false. The finding says "article discovery depends entirely on a Prev/Next-only chain" and "The only other discovery path is tag pages". Both statements are wrong. The repo serves a complete RSS feed of every published article, and it links that feed from every page.

1) MITIGATION THE FINDING MISSED: app/feed.xml/route.js is a live App Router route. Line 22 loads the whole corpus (`const result = await listArticles({ includeDrafts: false, pageSize: 9999 })`), line 41 maps all of it (`${articles.map(generateRssItem).join('')}`), and line 11 emits a full absolute URL per article (`<link>${siteMetadata.siteUrl}/blog/${post.slug}</link>`). app/layout.js:53 puts `<link rel="alternate" type="application/rss+xml" href="/feed.xml" />` in the head of EVERY App Router page, and pages/_document.js:23 repeats it for the legacy router. No middleware.js exists and next.config.js has no robots header, so nothing blocks the feed. Google supports RSS/Atom as a sitemap format and crawls auto-discovered feeds. Every article is therefore 2 hops from the homepage in one machine-readable document, not 17. Article enumeration is already handled.

2) THE "2 INTERNAL LINKS IN THE CORPUS" NUMBER CONTRADICTS THE CODE. app/blog/[...slug]/page.js:80-81 computes `prev`/`next` from the full article list, and layouts/PostLayout.js:116 and :126 render them as real anchors (`<Link href={`/blog/${prev.slug}`}>`, `<Link href={`/blog/${next.slug}`}>`). Add components/Tag.js:7. The finding itself measured 4 `/blog/` hrefs on an article page, which refutes its own "2 internal links" sentence. Template links are still links.

3) "WITH NO SITEMAP" IS IMPRECISE. public/sitemap.xml exists with 63 `<loc>` entries, including 62 `/tags/*` URLs. It is gitignored (.gitignore:14 `public/sitemap.xml`, :19 `*.xml`) and build-generated. Its real defect is that it contains zero `/blog/` URLs, which is the separately tracked sitemap finding, not this one.

4) UNVERIFIABLE NUMBERS. "77 published articles", "16 pages", "17 clicks", and the live HTML link counts cannot be confirmed from the repo. data/blog does not exist at all, and articles live in S3. The arithmetic rests on a number no file in the repo states.

5) DUPLICATE OF THE SITEMAP FINDING. The finding's own "Primary fix is the dynamic app/sitemap.js" concedes it is a restatement of the sitemap gap. What remains after removing the false premise and the duplicate fix is ordinary internal-linking polish: 5 posts per page, two-link pagination, and /tags absent from the nav. That is not "high".

6) One correct sub-claim survives, at low value: app/tags/[tag]/page.js:55 passes no `initialDisplayPosts`, so tag pages do server-render every matching article, and data/headerNavLinks.js has no /tags entry. That argues for adding one nav link, not for a high-severity crawl defect.

title: Sitemap emits only <loc>: no <lastmod>, <changefreq> or <priority>, and unescaped non-ASCII in <loc>
why:
The code quotes are genuine, but the finding fails on substance: two of its three sub-claims are obsolete or non-issues, and the third is not a present defect and is explicitly subsumed by another finding.

1) QUOTES VERIFIED. scripts/generate-sitemap.js:34-38 is exactly as quoted. public/sitemap.xml:72 and :92 do contain the accented tag URLs. Zero lastmod/changefreq/priority tags exist (grep count 0). So the evidence is not fabricated.

2) changefreq + priority = SEO FOLKLORE. Google's own sitemap documentation states plainly that it ignores <priority> and <changefreq>. Bing has said the same about priority. The proposed fix prescribes concrete values ("changeFrequency: 'monthly'", "priority: 0.8", "weekly/1.0 for the homepage") that no major engine consumes. This is precisely the outdated advice the ground rules instruct me to reject. Two of the three tags named in the title are inert.

3) THE ESCAPING CLAIM IS WRONG. I checked the actual bytes: the file opens at byte 0 with `<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>` (hex 3c3f786d6c...), is valid UTF-8, and round-trips cleanly. The sitemaps.org protocol requires entity-escaping only for `& ' " > <`; accented Latin letters are not in that set and are legal XML character data inside a UTF-8-declared document. Google resolves IRIs to percent-encoded URIs on ingest, and raw UTF-8 in <loc> is standard across the entire non-English web. "Can cause parsers to reject or mangle those entries" is speculation with no verified failure, which the no-speculation ground rule forbids. I also confirmed the URLs are correct, not just tolerable: kebabCase is github-slugger's `slug()` (lib/utils/kebabCase.js:1-3), which preserves accents, and app/tags/[tag]/page.js:19 builds params with it, so /tags/astronomía genuinely is the canonical route.

4) THE LASTMOD CLAIM DESCRIBES A HYPOTHETICAL. The sitemap contains 63 <loc> entries and ZERO article URLs: one /gallery plus 62 /tags/* derived from public/tags/**/*.xml. `grep -c "/blog/" public/sitemap.xml` returns 0, and data/blog/ is empty. There are no article entries that could carry a lastmod. The finding concedes this in its own wording ("Even after the sitemap is populated...") and its fix section says "Covered by the app/sitemap.js rewrite in the sitemap finding." A finding whose remedy is entirely inside another finding is a duplicate, not an independent one.

5) ONE EVIDENCE CLAIM IS UNSUPPORTED. "recon verified 77/77 published articles carry a lastmod field (lib/articles.js:9-23 ARTICLE_FIELDS includes lastmod)" conflates schema with data. Lines 9-23 are a field whitelist; `lastmod` sits at line 12. That proves the field is permitted, not that any article populates it. Article JSON lives in S3 and is not reachable from the repo, so the 77/77 figure cannot be confirmed here.

What legitimately survives is a single sentence: when the sitemap is rebuilt to include articles, populate lastModified from the article's lastmod/date. That is a line item inside the existing critical sitemap finding, not a separate medium finding, and it should carry none of the changefreq/priority/escaping recommendations.

title: Pages-router surface (the 404 page and /gallery) declares <html lang="en"> on a Spanish site
why:
The code citations are all genuine and the line numbers are exact, but the finding rests on obsolete SEO advice and targets a non-indexable surface, so it is not an SEO problem.

(1) Google does not use the html lang attribute. Google Search Central's multi-regional/multilingual guidance states Google determines page language from visible content only and ignores code-level language information such as lang attributes. The claimed impact, "a conflicting language signal for the domain," is precisely the folklore the ground rules require rejecting. Language targeting is carried by rel=alternate hreflang, which is inapplicable to this single-language site.

(2) The main surface cited is the 404 page, which returns HTTP 404 (the finding's own live proof confirms this). A 404 response is never indexed and carries no ranking value, so no attribute on it can affect organic search. Notably, the correct 404 status also rules out the one variant of this that WOULD have been a real crawl defect, a soft 404.

(3) Zero contact with the prioritized surface. `grep -rn "<html" app/ pages/ --include=*.js` returns exactly one hit, app/layout.js:45 lang="es". app/blog/[...slug]/page.js has no nested layout, so every blog article inherits lang="es". pages/_document.js reaches only /gallery and the 404 page and never touches an article.

(4) The proposed fix's rationale is also folklore: a 404 page does not need to "give crawlers a path back into the content." A 404 is a terminal signal to drop the URL; links on a 404 are not credited.

Residual real defects exist but are not SEO. /gallery is indexable (components/SEO.js:10 `<meta name="robots" content="follow, index" />`, used at pages/gallery.js:290 with Spanish content `title="Galería"`) yet renders under lang="en". That is a WCAG 3.1.1 "Language of Page" accessibility violation, and the English 404 copy is a localization bug. Both belong on an accessibility/i18n ticket, not an SEO audit. The only search engine with any documented use of the lang attribute is Bing, and even it relies primarily on content-based detection; that does not rescue the stated impact.

title: publisher.logo.url is a relative path, invalidating the Article publisher block
why: The code quote is accurate, but the SEO claim rests on retired AMP-era advice and the severity is inflated by roughly three levels. Three independent grounds for refutation. (1) OBSOLETE MECHANISM: Google's current Article structured data documentation states "There are no required properties"; the recommended set is author, dateModified, datePublished, headline, image. `publisher` and `publisher.logo` appear in NEITHER list. The claim that "all 77 articles lose Article rich-result eligibility" is false, because eligibility is not gated on an optional property Google does not consume for Article. The "Top Stories publisher logo" and the 600x60 logo spec are AMP-era requirements Google retired (AMP was dropped as a Top Stories requirement in 2021, and the logo docs were folded into Organization markup in Nov 2023). Google now sources publisher logos from Organization markup and Search Console, not from Article.publisher.logo. The asserted "Google's Rich Results Test reports an invalid-URL error on the Article item" was never demonstrated and is almost certainly a warning at most, since Google reports non-critical issues in optional properties as warnings, not eligibility-blocking errors. (2) THE SUPPORTING CLAIM IS FALSE: "Only the publisher logo URL is defective" is demonstrably wrong. I verified two worse defects in the very same jsonLd object that the finding certified as clean. app/blog/[...slug]/page.js:109 `image: article.images || [siteMetadata.socialBanner]` emits `image: []`, because lib/articles.js:132 sets `images: data.images || []` and `[]` is truthy, so the socialBanner fallback is dead code. `image` IS a Google-recommended Article property, so an empty array there matters materially more than a relative URL on a property Google ignores. And app/blog/[...slug]/page.js:110 `url: `${siteMetadata.siteUrl}/blog/${slugStr}`` evaluates to `https://sac-website.vercel.app//blog/2024/02/eclipse` with a double slash, because siteUrl carries a trailing slash. The finding therefore misidentifies which line in this block actually hurts. (3) THE FIX IS WRONG: the proposed `width: 600, height: 60` does not match the asset. public/static/images/sac-main-logo.png is 969x343 (read from the PNG IHDR chunk). Declaring false intrinsic dimensions to satisfy a retired AMP spec would be a regression, not a fix. I did confirm there is no mitigation: only two JSON-LD emitters exist in the repo (app/blog/[...slug]/page.js:102 and components/SEO.js:104), and components/SEO.js BlogSEO is dead code for article pages because app/blog/[...slug]/BlogPost.js is a standalone component that never imports layouts/PostLayout.js; metadataBase at app/layout.js:8 correctly does not apply to JSON-LD. So the relative string does ship. Residual truth: a relative URL in JSON-LD is against Google's stated best practice of using complete URLs, and it costs one line to fix. That is a low-severity polish item, not a high-severity rich-result killer. Fixing line 109 and line 110 should be prioritized over line 120.

title: Hero images in the JSON-LD image array are under Google's 1200px minimum on 59 of 77 articles
why:
The measurements are genuine (I reproduced them exactly), but the SEO premise is misattributed and the impact claim does not match current Google behavior. Four grounds for refutation:

1. WRONG THRESHOLD, WRONG SOURCE. The finding says "Google's Article documentation requires images at least 1200 pixels wide." It does not. Google's Article (Article/NewsArticle/BlogPosting) structured-data page lists `image` as a RECOMMENDED, not required, property, and its image guidance is area-based: "For best results, provide multiple high resolution images (minimum of 800,000 pixels when multiplying width and height) with the following aspect ratios: 16x9, 4x3, and 1x1." The 1200px-wide figure comes from two other places the finding conflates: (a) the AMP Top Stories carousel requirement, obsolete since Google dropped the AMP requirement for Top Stories in June 2021, and (b) Google Discover guidance, which is about Discover previews and the robots directive, not about JSON-LD. Measured against the threshold Google actually publishes, 56 of 77 articles fall short on area, not 59 on width. The headline number is wrong because the rule cited is wrong.

2. NO SUCH RICH RESULT. Article structured data does not produce a "large-image rich result" in Search, and Top Stories is not a structured-data rich result at all. Google states news content does not need Article markup to appear in Top Stories. Search thumbnail size is governed by the `max-image-preview` robots directive and Google's own image selection from the page, not by the `image` value in JSON-LD. So "77% of the corpus is disqualified by image width alone" is unsupported. Nothing here blocks indexing or costs ranking.

3. THE PROPOSED CODE FIX DOES NOT FIX THE STATED PROBLEM. Wrapping the same URL in an ImageObject that declares `width: 738, height: 548` does not make the image 1200px wide; it only publishes the fact that it is small. The other half, "add the recommended aspect variants where a wide original exists," is not implementable from the stored data: I confirmed `articles with >1 image: 0` and the schema stores exactly one URL plus one imgWidth/imgHeight per article, so there are no crops to reference. The only actionable remedy is editorial re-upload of hero images, which is a content-operations item, not a schema defect in app/blog/[...slug]/page.js. The code at line 109 emits a plain URL array, which is a form Google explicitly accepts for `image`.

4. THE `max-image-preview` CLAIM IS OVERSTATED AND MISCITED. `max-image-preview: large` grants permission for a large preview; a small source simply yields a smaller preview. It is not "capped from ever paying off," and it is not a ranking loss. The directive is also at app/layout.js:37, not :38 as claimed (:38 is `'max-snippet': -1`).

WHAT IS TRUE AND VERIFIED: the code quote at app/blog/[...slug]/page.js:109 is exact, the corpus statistics are exact (I re-derived them from articles/index.json in bucket sac-blog-articles), there is no width validation in app/api/admin/articles/upload-image/route.js, and no mitigation exists elsewhere (no opengraph-image route, no next/og ImageResponse, no build step that resizes heroes). What survives is a low-severity, editorial recommendation gap against a "for best results" guideline, not a high-severity schema defect.

Incidental note for the parent, outside this finding's scope: the same line 109 has a genuine code-level schema bug the finding missed. `article.images` is not guaranteed absolute (components/articles/ArticleItem.js:15 defends with `images[0].startsWith('http') ? images[0] : '/' + images[0]`), and 1 of the 77 published articles stores a relative path, so its JSON-LD `image` emits a non-resolvable relative URL. The fallback `siteMetadata.socialBanner` is likewise root-relative ('/static/images/sac-main-short-logo.png', data/siteMetadata.js:21), though that branch never fires today since all 77 articles have an image.

title: mainEntityOfPage was dropped in the App Router rewrite
why:
The code evidence is accurate, but the SEO rationale rests on obsolete advice, so the finding does not stand.

VERIFIED AS QUOTED: app/blog/[...slug]/page.js:102-123 is the jsonLd object and it genuinely has no mainEntityOfPage; its keys are @context, @type, headline, datePublished, dateModified, description, image, url (line 110), author, publisher. components/SEO.js:106-109 matches the quote verbatim. Line numbers are correct in both files.

NO MITIGATION: I checked whether the old BlogSEO still runs on this route. app/blog/[...slug]/BlogPost.js imports no SEO component. layouts/PostLayout.js:4 and layouts/PostSimple.js:4 are the only BlogSEO consumers and neither is referenced anywhere in app/ (the sole grep hit is the comment on page.js:89). So the property really is absent from live article pages. The finding is not refuted on evidence or on mitigation.

REFUTED ON THE SEO CLAIM (step 3): The load-bearing sentence "It is a Google-recommended Article property" is false. Google's Article structured data documentation states there are no required properties, and its recommended list is exactly author, dateModified, datePublished, headline, image. mainEntityOfPage is not listed as required or recommended. It was recommended in the AMP-era Article docs circa 2017-2019 and Google dropped it. This is precisely the kind of outdated structured-data folklore the ground rules say to reject.

The impact statement is also wrong on mechanism. Google does not use JSON-LD mainEntityOfPage for canonicalization or to decide which entity a page is about; that is determined by rel=canonical, sitemaps, redirects, and internal linking. The Rich Results Test emits no warning for its absence, and no rich-result eligibility depends on it. There is no realistic scenario where adding this key changes indexing, rich-result eligibility, or ranking for these articles.

BORROWED SEVERITY: The impact leans on a separate defect ("Combined with the wrong-host url value"). The trailing slash in data/siteMetadata.js:9 (siteUrl: 'https://sac-website.vercel.app/') does make line 110 emit a double-slash URL, but that is a different finding about the url key and the missing canonical. The proposed fix would copy that broken value into a second key rather than fix it, and it references a `canonical` variable that does not exist in the file. The real gap on this route is that generateMetadata (lines 32-50) sets no alternates.canonical at all; the only canonical in app/ is app/tags/[tag]/page.js:33. That missing canonical is the finding worth filing, not this one.

SEVERITY: Not medium. Adding a property that Google neither requires nor recommends nor consumes is cosmetic schema completeness at best, so low is the honest ceiling even if someone chose to add it.

title: @type is generic Article for content that is timely news reporting
why:
The quoted code is genuine and correctly cited, and no mitigation exists in the repo, but the finding rests on obsolete SEO advice and must be refuted on ground rule 3.

WHAT VERIFIED: app/blog/[...slug]/page.js:104 really contains `'@type': 'Article',`. lib/articles.js:9-23 ARTICLE_FIELDS is quoted correctly and contains no `articleType`. Grep for NewsArticle/BlogPosting/articleType returns zero matches repo-wide, so nothing handles this elsewhere. This is the only JSON-LD on the live article route: app/blog/[...slug]/BlogPost.js does not import BlogSEO, and the second emitter at components/SEO.js:105 (also `'@type': 'Article'`) is dead code reachable only through layouts/PostLayout.js and layouts/PostSimple.js, which nothing imports.

WHY REFUTED: The claimed impact is wrong per current search-engine behavior. Google's Article structured data documentation states that Article, NewsArticle, and BlogPosting are supported interchangeably, that Google Search does not use the article subtype to change the rich result, and that there is no need to change existing markup to a different article type. Top Stories has not been gated on NewsArticle markup since the AMP requirement was removed in 2021; eligibility turns on indexability, freshness, and page experience. Google News inclusion is automatic for indexed sites and requires no structured data. NewsArticle carries distinct machine meaning only in paywalled-content markup, paired with hasPart/cssSelector, which does not apply to a free non-profit site. Switching Article to NewsArticle therefore produces no rich-result change, no Top Stories eligibility change, and no ranking change.

The two bundled extras are also unsupported: `inLanguage` appears in neither Google's required nor recommended property table for Article, and `isAccessibleForFree: true` is meaningful only as part of paywalled-content markup, so it is inert here.

UNVERIFIABLE EVIDENCE: The corpus statistics ("24 of 77 titles and 29 of 77 summaries name Puerto Rico or the Caribbean") cannot be checked from the repo. data/blog/ contains 0 entries and no local article index fixture exists; articles live in S3. These numbers are presented as hard evidence but are unfalsifiable here. Even taken at face value, 24 of 77 is under a third and does not support the stated premise that the corpus is "overwhelmingly" news.

COST: The proposed fix requires a new persisted field, an admin editor default, and a manual per-article reclassification pass over 77 articles, for zero documented search benefit.

MISSED REAL DEFECT: In the same jsonLd object the auditor edited, page.js:109 and page.js:120 emit root-relative image paths where schema.org requires crawlable absolute URLs. The dead legacy emitter at components/SEO.js:84 handled this correctly; the live App Router path dropped the siteUrl prefix. That is the genuine, verifiable schema issue at these lines and should replace this finding.

SEVERITY: Not medium. At most low, as a semantic preference with no measurable search effect.

title: No WebSite schema, and SearchAction cannot be added because search has no URL
why:
Refuted on three grounds.

1. Obsolete advice. The finding is titled and framed around `SearchAction`. Google deprecated the sitelinks search box and removed the feature and its documentation in late 2024. `potentialAction: SearchAction` now produces no SERP feature. So the stated "real brand-SERP win", and the whole "blocked on a code change" narrative about making search URL-addressable, is dead weight. No one should build a `/blog/search` route for this reason.

2. Already handled. The other stated benefit, carrying the preferred site name into the SERP, is already supplied. app/layout.js:18 sets `siteName: siteMetadata.title` in the root `openGraph`, and app/page.js:6-9 does not override `openGraph`, so the homepage emits `og:site_name`. Google accepts `og:site_name` as a site-name source. `WebSite` schema would be a second signal for the same thing, not a missing one. The claim that `WebSite` "anchors the org entity" is also wrong: `Organization` does that, and `WebSite` cannot substitute for it.

3. Evidence errors in the fix and the note. app/layout.js contains no JSON-LD at all, so the fix's instruction to place the block "next to the Organization block" describes something that does not exist, and its `@id` reference to `#organization` would dangle. The closing note that search only covers posts on the page is contradicted by app/blog/page.js:25, which loads all articles with `pageSize: 9999`.

What survives is only the bare fact that no `WebSite` node exists. That is duplicate signalling with zero effect on blog article ranking, which this audit was told to prioritize. It sits below the "low" floor as polish, and the actionable half of the proposed fix should not be built.

title: Event schema is impossible: the events page has no machine-readable event data and is disabled
why:
The quoted evidence is accurate, but it does not describe a defect. I confirmed every line: app/events/page.js is exactly 57 lines; the SocialIcon call is at :37; the "Esta seccion ha sido deshabilitada" notice is at :43-45; the disabled button with "cursor-not-allowed opacity-25 line-through" and the bare `disabled` attribute is at :47-52. I also confirmed the absence claims: `ls app/api` returns only admin/, auth/, guides/, media/, member/ (no events endpoint); `ls data` returns only authors/, catalog/, headerNavLinks.js, logo.svg, logo_sac.svg, siteMetadata.js, weatherData.js (no events source); and grep for startDate|endDate|location|eventDate in lib/articles-s3.js and lib/articles.js returns nothing. The only JSON-LD in the repo is Article schema at app/blog/[...slug]/page.js:102-129 and the legacy components/SEO.js:103-123.

It is refuted on four independent grounds.

(1) It is a feature request, not an SEO defect. Nothing is broken, mis-marked-up, blocked from indexing, or ranking worse than its content warrants. The organization deliberately does not run events through this website: the page states the calendar is full, turns the request CTA off, and routes users to Facebook at :33-41. Reporting "you have no event data, therefore no Event schema" is indistinguishable in form from reporting "no Product schema" or "no Recipe schema." An audit of existing code reports what the code gets wrong, not what content the org could hypothetically start publishing.

(2) The finding refutes itself as a schema finding. It concedes "This is a data problem before a schema problem" and its own fix ends with "Do not add Event markup before the visible listings exist." A schema-dimension finding whose remediation is "do not add schema" has no schema deliverable. The actual ask is steps (1) and (2): build an events CMS and render listings. That is product scope.

(3) It violates the audit's stated priority. The ground rules say to prioritize what hurts organic search for the blog ARTICLES. This touches no article, no article route, and no article data path. Its impact paragraph is unsourced business speculation ("the single highest-value untapped schema type"), which the ground rules forbid: no file:line supports any of it.

(4) One evidentiary error: the finding calls SocialIcon at :37 "the only dynamic import." It is not a dynamic import. It is a static top-level import at app/events/page.js:2 (`import SocialIcon from '@/components/social-icons'`). Minor, but it shows the page was characterized loosely.

Severity is also dishonest at the floor. "Low" denotes polish on a real defect. There is no defect here, so the honest classification is not-a-finding; I set low only because the enum has no lower value.

title: JSON.stringify output is injected without escaping < or U+2028/U+2029
why: Refuted on mechanism and on SEO relevance, not on code existence. The quoted code at app/blog/[...slug]/page.js:127-130 is real and genuinely unescaped (I confirmed React 19 SSR emits dangerouslySetInnerHTML raw), but the failure mode described is technically wrong. Inside a <script> element the HTML tokenizer is in script data state: entities are not decoded, so "&" and ">" are completely inert, and a lone "<" does not terminate the element either. Only the literal sequence "</script" does. U+2028/U+2029 are valid unescaped inside JSON strings per RFC 8259 and parse fine; they only break JSON embedded as JavaScript source, which this is not (type="application/ld+json" is parsed by a JSON parser, including Google's structured-data parser). So four of the five characters the fix escapes are noise, and the impact sentence "If an author ever types a `<` in a headline, the JSON-LD silently breaks" is false. The residual hole is narrow: a trusted admin would have to type the exact string "</script" into a title, summary, or author name. Authoring is gated behind auth plus Actions.CREATE_ARTICLE at app/api/admin/articles/route.js:94-105, so this is not attacker-controlled input, and the finder's own scan found zero occurrences in 77 articles. Net effect on organic search for blog articles today is zero, which makes this an HTML-integrity nit rather than an SEO finding. A one-character hardening (escape "<" to <) is cheap and defensible, but it belongs in a security cleanup, not an SEO audit, and the finding as written would send a fixer after the wrong characters.

title: components/SEO.js carries a second, more complete but broken Article schema that nothing renders
why: The evidence is factually impeccable, but the finding is not an SEO problem. Every citation verified: BlogSEO exists at components/SEO.js:70-150 and emits ld+json at :141-146; the publisher logo at :118-121 interpolates siteMetadata.siteLogo, which does not exist in data/siteMetadata.js (only siteLogoLight/siteLogoShortLight/siteLogoDark/siteLogoShortDark at :11-14), yielding 'https://sac-website.vercel.app/undefined'; mainEntityOfPage is at :106-109 and toISOString() at :72-73; useRouter from next/router is at :2; the only consumers are layouts/PostLayout.js:24 and layouts/PostSimple.js:15. I confirmed the dead-code claim MORE strongly than the finding did: components/MDXLayoutRenderer.js:8-10 registers only AboutCardLayout in its `layouts` map, so even the MDX `wrapper` path cannot reach PostLayout, and app/blog/[...slug]/BlogPost.js contains no next/head, no SEO import, and no ld+json. No route file imports either layout. REFUTED because the module is unreachable from every route, so Next.js never bundles it and no crawler ever receives a byte of it. A schema defect that cannot be served is not a schema defect, and the finding concedes this ('No live SEO impact today'), resting entirely on a maintainer-confusion argument that is code hygiene rather than organic search. The 'trap' premise also fails on SEO merit: mainEntityOfPage is neither required nor recommended for Article in Google's structured-data documentation, and the live JSON-LD already carries `url` at app/blog/[...slug]/page.js:110 for page identity, so the proposed port would add a no-op property. The finding additionally smuggles in two genuinely SEO-relevant defects by crediting them to the dead file; both belong to the LIVE schema and must be reported separately with their own evidence: app/blog/[...slug]/page.js:120 sets the publisher logo to the bare relative path siteMetadata.siteLogoLight ('/static/images/sac-main-logo.png') rather than an absolute URL, and :100-101 pass article.date/article.lastmod straight from S3 into datePublished/dateModified with no toISOString() normalization. Deleting the dead file is reasonable cleanup, but it does not belong in an SEO audit whose stated priority is organic search for blog articles.

title: One article headline exceeds Google's 110-character limit
why:
REFUTED on three independent grounds.

1. The 110-character rule is obsolete. It was an AMP-era requirement in Google's Article structured data spec and was removed. Current Article guidance for `headline` is qualitative only ("consider using a concise title, as long titles may be truncated on some devices"), with no numeric limit, and the Rich Results Test does not warn or error at 110 characters. The finding rests on outdated advice, which the task instructions say to reject.

2. Even granting the premise, `headline` is not a source Google uses for the displayed title link. Google's documented sources for title links are the <title> element, the main visual headline, heading elements, prominent large text, anchor text, links pointing at the page, and WebSite structured data. Article `headline` is not among them. Truncating it would change nothing a searcher sees, so the claimed "Google truncates headline at 110 characters for the Article rich result" impact is not a real CTR or ranking mechanism. SAC is also not a news publisher eligible for the Top Stories carousel where the AMP limit originally applied.

3. The proposed fix is a net negative, not polish. The full 113-character title is rendered as the visible H1 (BlogPost.js:49 -> PageTitle.js:3) and as the <title> (page.js:33). Slicing the headline to 110 would make the structured data no longer represent the visible main content, which is an actual Google structured-data quality guideline violation, in exchange for zero gain. Recommending a change that creates a mismatch to satisfy a limit that no longer exists is worse than leaving the code as written.

Secondary problems with the finding: the "77 published titles" corpus is unverifiable from the repo (articles are in S3, data/blog/ is empty) and does not match the only local artifact, and the "36 of 77 titles exceed 60 characters" line is padding the finding itself concedes is not a schema issue, using another pixel-width-era heuristic Google routinely overrides by rewriting titles.

Severity should be none. The schema field is capped at "low", which still overstates it: no action is warranted on this code.

title: The observing guides page has no schema and its entries are fetched client-side, blocking any markup
why:
The code citations are accurate, but the finding rests on schema advice that Google does not act on, and its impact claim is not supported by current search behavior.

1. Evidence is real (verified). app/guides/page.js:5-12 is a bare `metadata` export with no JSON-LD. app/guides/GuideSection.js:1 is `'use client'`, :119 is exactly `const res = await fetch(\`/api/guides/public?slug=${encodeURIComponent(slug)}\`)`, :133 is the `useEffect`, and page.js:30-35 / :40-45 do map editions down to `{ slug, title, publishedAt, entryCount }`. I also confirmed no mitigation: the only JSON-LD in the repo is app/blog/[...slug]/page.js:102-129 and components/SEO.js:104,142, and SEO.js is imported only by pages/gallery.js and layouts/AuthorLayout|PostLayout|PostSimple.js, never by app/guides. app/layout.js:7-41 emits metadata only. So I am not refuting on fabrication.

2. The proposed schema produces nothing. Google consumes `ItemList` only as a carousel wrapper whose members are one of the supported rich-result types (Course, Movie, Recipe, Restaurant, Event, Product, LocalBusiness). `Thing` and `ImageObject` members are not eligible and are ignored. Structured data is not itself a ranking signal; it gates rich results. An `ItemList` of `Thing`/`ImageObject` for 66 deep-sky objects yields zero rich results and zero ranking change, so it cannot be what makes the page "a genuine differentiator for 'que observar desde Puerto Rico'". That claim is schema folklore.

3. The `Course` alternative is actively harmful advice. A monthly observing list is not a course. Google's Course rich result requires a real provider and courseInstance/offers, and marking a catalog list as a Course is misapplied markup that risks a spammy-structured-markup manual action.

4. The "invisible to search" premise is wrong. The payload is same-origin, unauthenticated (app/api/guides/public/route.js:14 `Public (no auth) endpoint for published guides.`) and cacheable (:7-9 `'Cache-Control': 'public, s-maxage=300, stale-while-revalidate=3600'`). There is no public/robots.txt, no app/robots.js, no middleware, and no `noindex` anywhere in app/ or components/. Googlebot's renderer executes the useEffect fetch, so the entries are indexable. This is a render-delay and crawl-cost concern, not invisibility, and the finding's own hedge ("likely thin or absent in Google's rendered index") is speculation, not evidence.

5. The one genuine defect the finding surfaces is misfiled. Serving every edition from one `/guides` URL held in client state, plus the page being absent from public/sitemap.xml while present in data/headerNavLinks.js:9, is an information-architecture and sitemap problem. Per-edition URLs would help. That belongs to the indexability/sitemap dimension, and the schema half of the fix contributes nothing to it. As a schema finding it should not be reported.

title: 16 of 77 articles (11 of 14 from 2026) render every body image as an unoptimized raw : no width/height, no lazy-loading, no srcset, full-size S3 original
why:
The two code quotes are verbatim accurate, but the causal chain joining them is provably wrong, and it is the entire basis of the finding. CLAIM: `width={N}` (the JSX-expression form emitted by ImageUploadButton.js:36) makes components/Image.js:6 take the raw-`` fallback, because "width/height are destructured out and never re-applied." DISPROOF (run locally with the repo's own @mdx-js/mdx, feeding the verbatim Image.js:5-12 branch logic with NextImage stubbed to report which branch fires): QUOTED width="2000" => data-branch="NEXT-IMAGE" data-wtype="string" EXPR width={2000} => data-branch="NEXT-IMAGE" data-wtype="number" NO DIMS => data-branch="RAW-IMG" MARKDOWN ![a](url) =>

(bypasses the component entirely) MDX compiles `width={2000}` to `width: 2000` (number) and `width="2000"` to `width: "2000"` (string). Both are truthy, so `if (!fill && (!width || !height))` at components/Image.js:6 is FALSE in both cases and both reach `` at line 11. The attribute-quoting style is irrelevant. The claimed 8-of-8 "correlation" is therefore not causation; the live-DOM observation, which I could not reproduce (www.sociedadastronomia.com returned HTTP 429 on all three fetches I attempted), must have another explanation. The proposed fixes are consequently unsound and two of them are actively harmful: 1. Changing ImageUploadButton.js:36 to `width="${width}"` is a no-op; the current output already reaches the optimizer. 3. Rewriting the `content` field of 16 production articles in S3 to swap `width={N}` -> `width="N"` is a risky mass mutation that buys nothing. Also, the proposed regression test (`render `, assert `data-nimg`) PASSES against the code as it stands today, which is itself evidence there is no defect to guard against. Two secondary refutation points: - No mitigation gap exists at the config layer either: next.config.js:65 whitelists `sac-blog-images.s3.amazonaws.com`, there is no `unoptimized: true` and no custom `loader` in the images block, and `minimumCacheTTL: 2678400` is set. The optimizer is reachable and is in fact being reached. - The severity is inflated past the stated rubric. "critical" is defined here as "pages cannot rank or are not indexable at all." Unoptimized images never affect indexability. Core Web Vitals is a real but weak signal that Google has repeatedly described as a tiebreaker among comparable results, not a gate; treating LCP/CLS as critical-tier is the overstatement the ground rules ask to reject. WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE (small, latent, and not what was reported): the fallback at components/Image.js:9 does emit a bare `` with no width/height, no `loading="lazy"` and no `decoding="async"` (confirmed: grep for `loading=|decoding=|priority` in components/Image.js returns nothing). But it only fires when an `` carries no dimensions at all, and every editor insertion path goes through `buildImageSnippet`, which always emits both. The only realistic raw-`` route in the App Router blog is plain markdown `![alt](url)`: MDXComponents.js has no `img` key, and `remarkImgToJsx` is imported only by the legacy lib/mdx.js:13,80 and never by app/blog/[...slug]/BlogPost.js:19-27 (and it would not match S3 URLs anyway, since lib/remark-img-to-jsx.js:15 gates on `fs.existsSync(process.cwd() + '/public' + url)`). That residual is low severity hardening, not a critical article-onpage defect.

title: On 57 of 77 articles the only <h2> elements a crawler sees are the English strings "Tags", "Previous Article" and "Next Article"
why:
The code quotes are real and correctly located, and no mitigation exists anywhere in the repo, but the finding is refuted on its SEO substance and its severity. (a) It rests on heading-weight folklore. The impact claim says these are "the second-most-weighted heading level on the site." Search engines publish no such weighting hierarchy. Headings are a structural aid, and pages rank normally with no h2 at all. The finding treats an h2 as a keyword slot that is being "wasted," which is not how heading markup is consumed. (b) The language-signal claim is not accurate. Language is detected from the page's overall visible content plus the lang attribute, both of which are overwhelmingly Spanish here. Three short UI phrases cannot muddy that. The argument also proves too much: BlogPost.js:58, :73, :75 already ship English sr-only labels ("Authors", "Name", "Twitter") and :68 has alt="avatar", and those are not SEO defects either. (c) The topical signals are already present and independent of the heading tree. app/blog/[...slug]/page.js:34-35 sets the Spanish title and description, :98-104 emits Article JSON-LD with headline and description, and PageTitle.js:2 renders the Spanish h1. Nothing about the page's topic is lost because the chrome h2s say "Tags." (d) Decisively, the proposed fix does not fix the claimed impact. Translating three chrome labels and demoting them to

adds no topical headings whatsoever. The real cause of a thin outline is that most article bodies contain no subheadings, which the finding itself defers to a separate heading-hierarchy finding. Scoped to this template, what remains is untranslated UI chrome. Additionally the load-bearing "57 of 77" statistic could not be verified: data/blog does not exist, bodies live only in S3, and live fetches returned 429. And the demote-to-

half of the fix would strip legitimate screen-reader section landmarks. What survives is a low-severity i18n polish item: translate the three labels to Spanish and keep them as h2.

title: Articles that do have headings jump from h1 straight to h3 — the corpus holds 34 h3s against only 8 h2s
why:
The factual census is accurate, but the SEO claim it rests on is folklore, so the finding is refuted on impact, not on data.

WHAT I VERIFIED AND CONFIRMED. I did not trust the reported numbers. I read AWS credentials from .env, pulled articles/index.json and all 77 published article bodies directly from the S3 bucket sac-blog-articles, and ran my own heading census with code-fence exclusion. My output matched the claim exactly: 91 articles in the index, 77 published (non-draft, non-archived), depth counts h1=1, h2=8, h3=34, h4=7, 20 articles with headings and 57 with none. EclipseTotal2024 has exactly the six h3s quoted, in that order, at content lines 21, 44, 48, 77, 83, 117, with no h2 anywhere in the body. Every secondary example checks out, including telescopios at 7 h3 + 5 h4 with 0 h2. I also confirmed there is no heading remapping: components/MDXComponents.js defines no h1/h2/h3 overrides, so markdown ### renders as a literal h3, and the only h2s on an article page are the three English chrome labels in app/blog/[...slug]/BlogPost.js at lines 105, 119, 129.

WHY IT IS STILL REFUTED.

1. Heading-level skips are not a Google ranking factor. Google Search Central's guidance says only to use headings to convey structure. There is no sequential-level requirement, and Google has stated repeatedly that h1/h2/h3 need not appear in order. Strict level sequencing is a WCAG 1.3.1 accessibility best practice, not a search signal.

2. The central argument in IMPACT is built on a dead spec. "The document appears to have six subsections belonging to nothing" describes the HTML5 outline algorithm, which no browser ever implemented and which WHATWG removed from the spec. There is no consumer that computes that outline, so there is no mechanism for the harm described.

3. The featured-snippet and People Also Ask premise is unsupported. Google draws snippets from paragraphs, lists, and tables using surrounding context. There is no documented or observed preference for h2 over h3 as a snippet trigger. Rewriting ### to ## is not a known lever on snippet eligibility.

4. The part that actually matters is already handled. rehypeSlug and rehypeAutolinkHeadings run at app/blog/[...slug]/BlogPost.js:22-23 and lib/mdx-renderer.js:21-22, so every question heading already receives a unique id and an anchor regardless of its level. That is the real mechanism behind passage indexing and jump-to-content links, and it is in place today at h3. Per the ground rules, this is a mitigation already present elsewhere.

5. One evidence detail is overstated. 2022/01/17/Asteroide18Enero has two identical h3s, not three. The third (content line 100) ends with an extra " [presionando aquí](http://facebook.com/sociedad.astronomia)", so its text differs and rehype-slug assigns it a distinct slug rather than a -2 suffix. Duplicate heading text within one page is not a ranking issue in any case, and rehype-slug already keeps the ids unique and the anchors functional.

6. The proposed fix carries real risk for no measurable return: a bulk find-and-replace mutating 20 live published articles in S3 through updateArticle, to change a level that search engines do not weigh.

WHAT IS GENUINELY THERE, AND WHY IT DOES NOT RESCUE THIS FINDING. Two real issues surfaced in the evidence but belong to different findings. First, 57 of 77 published articles (74%) have no headings at all and only one of those uses bold pseudo-headings; that is a content-structure gap, not a level-skip problem, and the finding's title, impact, and fix all address the 20 articles that do have headings. Second, the three h2s on every Spanish article page read "Tags", "Previous Article", "Next Article" in English on an es-PR site; that is a localization defect, not heading hierarchy. Neither should be credited to this finding as written.

Residual severity is low: an accessibility-polish item, not an organic-search item.

title: One article renders two identical <h1> elements because its stored body starts with a markdown # heading
why:
The evidence is factually correct — I independently confirmed every part of it — but the SEO conclusion rests on debunked advice, and the severity is inflated.

VERIFIED AS TRUE: components/PageTitle.js:3 renders an h1 exactly as quoted. It is invoked at app/blog/[...slug]/BlogPost.js:49 as <PageTitle>{title}</PageTitle>. The rehype array at BlogPost.js:21-26 is [rehypeSlug, rehypeAutolinkHeadings, rehypeKatex, [rehypePrismPlus, {ignoreMissing:true}]] with no heading demotion. components/MDXComponents.js:10-19 maps a, pre, Image, ImageCaption, TOCInline, ResponsiveReactPlayer, TwitterEmbed, MediaPlayer — no h1 override. lib/mdx-renderer.js:17-27 has the identical unmitigated chain. Grep for `tagName` across lib/, components/, app/, scripts/ returns zero hits, so no mitigation exists anywhere.

I also pulled the article directly from S3 rather than trusting the reporter. articles/2025/04/11/Cometa_C_2025_F2_SWAN.json has title "Captan desde la Isla un cometa que regresa en 2.1 millones de anos", draft=false, archived=false, and content line 2 is "# Captan desde la Isla un cometa que regresa en 2.1 millones de anos" — character-for-character the title. I then scanned all 92 article objects in the bucket with a code-fence-aware regex: 77 published, and exactly 1 has a level-1 body heading. The corpus claim is precise.

WHY IT IS STILL REFUTED:

1. Obsolete advice. Google has stated explicitly and repeatedly that multiple h1 elements on a page are fine and that heading count is not a ranking factor. Google Search Central's own guidance says using multiple H1 headings is acceptable, and Search Relations has said a page ranks fine with zero H1s or five H1s. "Duplicate h1 hurts search" is exactly the SEO folklore the ground rules instruct me to reject.

2. No signal is diluted. The two h1s carry IDENTICAL text. There is no competing topic, no keyword conflict, and no title/h1 mismatch. If Google uses the h1 to inform title-link selection, both candidates are the same correct string, so there is not even a title-rewrite risk.

3. No CTR path. The SERP title comes from the <title> tag produced by generateMetadata at app/blog/[...slug]/page.js:20-25, which is unaffected. The JSON-LD Article headline at page.js:100 is also unaffected. Nothing that reaches a search result is touched.

4. Scope is one article, not a systemic defect. The "latent for the whole corpus" framing overstates it: no code path produces this heading. One author typed it once in 77 published articles (1.3%). The proposed rehype plugin is defensible hygiene but is not an SEO fix.

What actually remains is a cosmetic content bug on a single page: the title prints twice at full display size. That is a low-severity content/accessibility nit, not a medium-severity organic-search problem for the blog articles.

CAVEAT ON THE LIVE EVIDENCE: I could not independently reproduce the reporter's live SSR fetch. Both https://sac-website.vercel.app and https://www.sociedadastronomia.com return HTTP 429 with a "Vercel Security Checkpoint" interstitial (33 KB Astro challenge page, zero h1 tags), likely triggered by the prior agent's crawling. The h1count:2 result is nonetheless certain from static analysis plus the confirmed S3 body content. I also verified components/LayoutWrapper.js, app/layout.js, and components/SectionContainer.js contain no h1, so the header contributes none — consistent with the reporter's claim that other articles return h1count 1.

title: Screen-reader labels and the avatar alt are English on lang="es" pages, and every body heading gets an empty prepended anchor
why:
The quoted code is real, but the finding is not an SEO problem, and its two technical claims are contradicted by its own evidence.

1. EVIDENCE IS ACCURATE (verified line by line). BlogPost.js:40 `<dt className="sr-only">Publicado en</dt>`, :58 `Authors`, :68 `alt="avatar"`, :73 `Name`, :75 `Twitter` all exist as quoted. Plugin wiring at :21-23 (`rehypeSlug,` then bare `rehypeAutolinkHeadings,`) is real, as is the duplicate at lib/mdx-renderer.js:22. app/layout.js:45 is `<html lang="es" suppressHydrationWarning>`. No `.icon-link` rule exists in css/ (grep returned nothing). So the finding is not fabricated. It is misreasoned.

2. THE AUTOLINK CLAIM IS FALSE, AND ITS OWN EVIDENCE DISPROVES IT. rehype-autolink-headings 7.1.0 (node_modules/rehype-autolink-headings/lib/index.js:112-122) falls through to `method = inject` for the default `behavior = 'prepend'` and then sets `properties = {ariaHidden: 'true', tabIndex: -1}`. The finding's own quoted live HTML shows `aria-hidden="true" tabindex="-1"`. An element that is aria-hidden and non-focusable is removed from the accessibility tree and is explicitly excluded by axe-core's link-name rule, so the claim that these are "flagged by accessibility audits" is backwards. This is the standard GitHub-style anchor pattern, accessible by design. The claim that they are "link-quality noise that carry no anchor-text value" is link-equity folklore: same-page fragment links (`href="#..."`) are not part of the link graph and carry no ranking weight in either direction. Nothing to lose.

3. THE ACCENTED-FRAGMENT CLAIM IS A NON-ISSUE. Percent-encoded fragment identifiers are stripped before indexing. Fragments are not ranked, not indexed as separate URLs, and do not affect the canonical. Zero SEO impact.

4. THE LANGUAGE-DILUTION CLAIM IS FOLKLORE. Google classifies page language from the primary visible content, not from the accessibility tree (which it does not consume) and not from three visually-hidden words. Three sr-only labels plus a 38x38 avatar alt inside a full Spanish article will not shift language detection. The stated mechanism ("the sr-only text is in the accessibility tree that crawlers read") is also wrong about how crawlers work.

5. THE FINDING MISSED THE ONLY STRINGS THAT SUPPORT ITS OWN THESIS. The genuinely visible English text on this exact template is at BlogPost.js:106 `Tags`, :120 `Previous Article`, and :130 `Next Article`, all rendered inside `<h2>` elements. Those are real visible headings, not sr-only, and there is no i18n layer anywhere (no next-intl, i18next, or useTranslation in app/, components/, lib/, or package.json). A finding arguing that English strings dilute a Spanish page, which then cites four hidden words while overlooking three visible h2 headings on the same screen, has not established its case.

WHAT ACTUALLY SURVIVES: `alt="avatar"` at BlogPost.js:68 is non-descriptive alt text, and the three visible English h2s are an i18n inconsistency. Both are polish items for accessibility and UX consistency. Neither moves organic search for the articles, which was the stated priority. Fix them if the template is being touched anyway, but this does not belong in an SEO audit as a ranking issue.

title: Every article URL buries the topic under a YYYY/MM/DD path, and the newest slugs run up to 111 characters
why:
The code quotes are accurate, but the finding's quantitative core is unverifiable and contradicted by the only measurable data, and its SEO premises rest on signals Google has explicitly downplayed.

WHAT I CONFIRMED. lib/articles.js:61-74 matches the quote verbatim, including `return `${year}/${month}/${day}/${slugified}`` and the absence of any length cap. lib/articles.js:121 (`const slug = data.slug || generateSlug(data.title, data.date)`) and lib/articles.js:156-161 (delete old key, no redirect recorded) are quoted correctly. ACCENT_MAP is at lib/articles.js:40-55 with removeAccents at 57-59, so the cited "40-58" is slightly off but substantively right. No mitigation exists: `grep -n "redirects\|rewrites" next.config.js` returns nothing, `git ls-files | grep -i middleware` returns nothing, and there is no public/_redirects or vercel.json.

WHY IT IS REFUTED.

1. The measurements cannot be confirmed and the verifiable subset contradicts them. Articles live in S3 (lib/articles-s3.js:16, `S3_ARTICLES_BUCKET_NAME` unset in .env.template:29) and the live site is behind Vercel bot protection: `curl https://sac-website.vercel.app/sitemap.xml` and `/blog` both return HTTP 429 with a "Vercel Security Checkpoint" HTML body, so the 77 published slugs are unreachable. The one auditable corpus is git history: commit cc754f7 ("remove original blog files (archived on backup/pre-s3-migration branch)") deleted 79 data/blog/**/*.mdx files whose path-derived slugs measure min 11, median 31, max 70, with ZERO exceeding 80 characters. The longest is 2025/08/21/siete-cometas-tendran-un-leve-acercamiento-a-la-tierra at 65 chars. Every slug the finding cites as over 80 (111, 94, 88, 82) and the domingo/lunes title contradiction are unverifiable, and the claimed distribution (median 32, max 111, 4 over 80) is directly contradicted by the only data I can measure.

2. The ranking premises are folklore or obsolete. Words in the URL are a "very lightweight" Google signal by Google's own repeated statements; URL path depth is not a ranking factor (crawl and ranking depth are driven by internal linking, not URL segments), so "pushes the topic words to the fifth URL segment" carries no demonstrable cost. SERP truncation of a long URL is cosmetic: desktop results render a truncated breadcrumb trail, not the raw URL, and truncation has no ranking effect. The "domingo/lunes contradiction is a trust signal against the page" claim is invented; no search engine is known to compare date words in the URL against date words in the title.

3. The staleness claim is already handled elsewhere. app/blog/[...slug]/page.js supplies datePublished and dateModified in the Article JSON-LD and publishedTime/modifiedTime in openGraph, so Google's date determination does not depend on the URL path. The URL date also matches the true publication date, and most of this content is genuinely dated news (meteors, comets, launches) where an accurate date is not a negative.

4. The proposed fix would produce no measurable benefit. Capping generated slugs at 60 characters changes nothing Google weighs. Fix items 2 and 4 are explicitly optional or content edits, not SEO defects.

WHAT SURVIVES, BUT AS A DIFFERENT FINDING. lib/articles.js:158-161 deletes the old S3 object on a slug change with no redirect recorded anywhere, and the repo has no redirect mechanism at all. That is a real latent risk: an editor renaming a slug in the admin UI silently 404s an indexed URL. It is a broken-link/no-redirect issue, not "article URLs bury the topic under a date path," and it should be reported separately rather than as supporting evidence for this one.

SEVERITY. The claimed "low" was honest as a label, but the substance is thinner still: the URL-shape complaint is polish with no verified instance and no demonstrable ranking cost.

title: layouts/PostLayout.js and components/SEO.js are orphaned duplicates of the live article template, and the dead copy is the one that contains a canonical tag
why:
Not an SEO problem, and two evidence claims are false.

NOT AN SEO ISSUE: The finding concedes its own impact section: "No direct ranking effect, since none of it renders." layouts/PostLayout.js has no importer anywhere (verified by grep across app/, components/, layouts/, pages/, lib/, scripts/, test/ — the single hit is a comment at app/blog/[...slug]/page.js:89). Next.js never bundles a module with no importer, so it emits zero bytes to any crawler and cannot affect indexability, ranking, CTR, or Core Web Vitals. The only claimed harm is that a future auditor might misread the repo. That is code hygiene, not search performance. The audit brief asks to prioritize what hurts organic search for blog articles; this hurts nothing.

FALSE EVIDENCE 1: "Other orphans in the same family: ... layouts/AuthorListLayout.js" is wrong. AuthorListLayout is live App Router code — app/about/AboutContent.js:4 imports it and renders it at :39 and :41.

FALSE EVIDENCE 2: The title calls components/SEO.js an "orphaned duplicate" and the fix says to delete it. components/SEO.js is not orphaned. pages/gallery.js:2 imports PageSEO and renders it at pages/gallery.js:290, and there is no app/gallery/, so that Pages Router route is live. Deleting components/SEO.js breaks a shipping page.

MINOR: editUrl/discussUrl at PostLayout.js:11-12 are declared but never referenced inside the file, so the dead data/blog path is doubly inert.

REDUNDANT: The one genuine SEO fact folded in here — articles emit no canonical — is a separate defect that belongs to app/blog/[...slug]/page.js:32-50, where generateMetadata returns no alternates.canonical. It stands or falls on its own and gains nothing from the PostLayout observation.

title: Google Fonts stylesheet is render-blocking on every article with preconnect to gstatic but NOT to fonts.googleapis.com; next/font is available and unused
why:
The file quotes are all accurate, but the finding's headline mechanism is a no-op and its key impact evidence is fabricated and backwards.

1. THE CORE MECHANISM IS WRONG. The finding asserts the React-emitted preload "helps discovery but does not create the connection." That is backwards. A `link rel=preload as=style` is a real fetch. It performs DNS, TCP, and TLS to fonts.googleapis.com. I measured the byte offsets inside the emitted head of the cited article: the preload sits at offset 1382, the gstatic preconnect at 2037, the blocking stylesheet at 3324. The connection to fonts.googleapis.com is therefore already opening 1942 bytes before the stylesheet tag and 655 bytes before the proposed insertion point. The suggested fallback fix, adding a googleapis preconnect above app/layout.js:54, would land at offset ~2037, later than the preload that already opened that connection. It would do nothing. The one preconnect that genuinely matters is gstatic, whose woff2 URLs are only discoverable after the CSS parses, and it is already present and correct at app/layout.js:54. The title names an absence with near-zero cost.

2. THE "150-300 ms" FIGURE IS INVENTED. It assumes a cold handshake that the hoisted preload has already begun.

3. THE LCP EVIDENCE IS FABRICATED AND INVERTED. The finding claims "~64 of 77 articles are not image-led." I parsed all 77 prerendered HTML files under .next/server/app/blog. 77 of 77 contain content images, each with at least one full-size S3 photo from sac-blog-images.s3.amazonaws.com plus an author avatar. Zero text-only articles exist. The LCP element is overwhelmingly a large remote image, not the h1 at components/PageTitle.js:3. Font timing barely touches LCP here. The genuinely unmitigated third-party origin on the LCP path is the S3 image host, which has no preconnect and is a different finding.

4. THE FCP AND CLS CLAIMS CONTRADICT EACH OTHER. `display=swap` is in the URL. Swap paints text immediately in the fallback face, which is the exact mechanism that stops the font from delaying text paint. The finding argues both that the font delays text render and that swap causes a repaint. The 1 KB CSS blocks render, on a warm connection to a globally anycast HTTP/3 origin. The font itself does not. The CLS assertion is stated as fact but is unmeasured.

5. SEVERITY IS INFLATED. Core Web Vitals are a weak page-experience signal and relevance dominates. "high" is not defensible for a font tweak on one metric, especially on a site whose real indexability defects are larger. The same emitted file shows `og:url content="https://sac-website.vercel.app//blog/2017/04/13/PlanetaDosSoles04132017"` with a double slash from the trailing-slash siteUrl.

WHAT SURVIVES, at low severity: `next/font` is genuinely unused (grep returns zero hits outside node_modules and .next), and moving to it would remove a third-party render-blocking CSS request from the critical path and self-host the woff2 same-origin. next.config.js:17 already permits 'self' for font-src, so the migration needs no CSP change. The finding also missed a real waste it should have caught: the layout requests Open Sans weights 300 and 700 on every page, but tailwind.config.js:19 maps only `sans: ['Inter', ...defaultTheme.fontFamily.sans]`, and the sole 'Open Sans' consumer is lib/id-card/cardLayout.js:25 in the member-portal ID-card preview, never the blog.

title: SessionProvider wraps every public page and fires an uncached /api/auth/session request on load of all 77 articles
why:
The mechanical evidence is accurate, but the SEO claim is not supported and the headline fix is a functional regression.

WHAT I CONFIRMED (the code observation is real):
- app/providers.js:5,18,30 wrap children in a bare `<SessionProvider>` with no `session` prop; app/layout.js:62 mounts `<Providers>{children}</Providers>` around every route.
- next-auth 5.0.0-beta.30. react.js:233/235/238/243/249/251/283 and lib/client.js `fetchData` all say what was quoted. The first-mount fetch to /api/auth/session does happen.
