- .next/static/chunks/7185-1dc8008327fa58e0.js exists (6,471 bytes raw), contains `__NEXTAUTH`/`getSession`/`csrfToken`, and is referenced by .next/server/app/blog/2017/04/13/PlanetaDosSoles04132017.html. 77 prerendered article HTML files exist.

WHY IT IS NOT AN SEO PROBLEM (the causal chain to organic search is absent):
1. Indexability: unaffected. All 77 articles are prerendered static HTML; content is in the markup and needs no JS.
2. CLS: I grepped all 19 `useSession` call sites. Every one is under app/admin/, components/admin/, or components/dashboard/. No public component consumes the session, so nothing shifts when it resolves. No CLS.
3. LCP: the fetch fires in a `React.useEffect` (react.js:243) after hydration. It is not on the render path.
4. INP: `setSession`/`setLoading` fire once, but `{children}` is a stable element reference passed as a prop from the server component, so React bails out of re-rendering the article subtree.
5. Payload: I measured the article page's 11 chunks at 679,050 bytes raw. The next-auth chunk is 6,471 raw / 2,609 gzip, i.e. 0.95% of page JS. Unmeasurable.
The remaining "extra serverless invocation" point is a hosting-cost concern, not a ranking or CTR concern. The finding's own impact text concedes "It is not the biggest single cost."

THE PROPOSED FIX IS HARMFUL: `session={null}` sets `hasInitialSession` true (react.js:233), so `_session` becomes null (:238). Every later refetch path then short-circuits on react.js:266 `__NEXTAUTH._session === null ||`, including the visibilitychange handler (:304-311) and the poll timer (:319-325, guarded by `if (__NEXTAUTH._session)`). A genuinely signed-in admin would see `status: "unauthenticated"` permanently. This would break app/admin/ and app/member/. Only the secondary suggestion (move SessionProvider into app/admin/layout.js and app/member/layout.js, both of which exist) is sound, and that is a code-hygiene cleanup, not an SEO fix.

title: S3 article reads are entirely uncached and duplicated per request, so a new article's first Googlebot crawl blocks on three sequential S3 round trips
why:
The code observation is real but it is a micro-optimization, not an SEO defect, and three pieces of the evidence are wrong.

VERIFIED AS ACCURATE: lib/articles-s3.js:78-102 getArticleIndex() does read S3 with no memoisation (the quoted :86-94 block is verbatim). lib/cache.js has exactly one importer, lib/google-sheets.js:4. Repo-wide greps for unstable_cache, revalidateTag, 'use cache', and `cache` imported from 'react' on the server return zero hits. app/blog/[...slug]/page.js:25, :64, :75 are exactly as quoted, with dynamicParams=true at :17 and revalidate=3600 at :18. No dynamic API in app/layout.js or components/LayoutWrapper.js forces the route dynamic. So there is no mitigation hiding elsewhere.

EVIDENCE ERRORS (3):
1. "77 prerendered entries" is wrong. .next/prerender-manifest.json contains 63 /blog/20* routes, not 77.
2. "three SEQUENTIAL S3 round trips" is wrong. In the App Router generateMetadata resolves concurrently with the page render, so the :25 getArticle overlaps the page body. The critical path is 2 sequential GetObject calls (:64 then :75), overstating latency by roughly 50%.
3. The MDX compile is misattributed. lib/mdx-renderer.js compileMDX has ZERO callers (dead code, confirmed by grep); the page calls only extractToc. The actual compile happens at app/blog/[...slug]/BlogPost.js:94 via next-mdx-remote/rsc.

WHY THE SEO CLAIM FAILS: The finding concedes its own scope. It admits the prerendered articles are unaffected, and the manifest confirms this (initialRevalidateSeconds 3600 with initialExpireSeconds 31536000 = stale-while-revalidate, which never blocks a visitor). All that remains is a single blocking render per newly published article. TTFB is not a Core Web Vital and not a Google ranking factor. Core Web Vitals are CrUX field data from real Chrome users, and every real user after that one cold render receives cached HTML, so the cold render never shapes the field measurement. Googlebot's fetch timeout is on the order of tens of seconds against a render of a few small same-region JSON GETs plus one MDX compile. Crawl budget is a documented concern only for very large or very rapidly changing sites, not for 63 articles. Finally, what actually gates first indexing of a new article on this site is URL discovery (the sitemap globs data/blog/**/*.mdx and matches nothing), not render latency; caching the S3 index does not change when Googlebot arrives.

This is a legitimate code-efficiency cleanup (the duplicate getArticle at :25 and :64, and pulling 9999 index entries at :75 just for two neighbours), and it belongs in a performance/refactor backlog. It does not belong in an SEO audit at medium severity, since no page ranks worse or indexes slower because of it.

title: Open Sans is requested in the site-wide font stylesheet but no public page uses it
why:
The quoted code all exists verbatim, but the finding's central claim, its impact model, and its fix are each wrong.

(1) TITLE IS FALSE. Open Sans IS used by a public page. `app/card-test-longname/page.js:52` renders `<IdCard cardData={cardData} />` on a fully public App Router route. No `middleware.js` exists anywhere in the repo (`find . -maxdepth 3 -name "middleware.*" -not -path "*/node_modules/*"` returns nothing), the page contains no auth call, no `noindex`, and nothing excludes it from the build. `IdCard.js:175` applies `CARD.FONT_FAMILY_BROWSER` whenever a style sets fontFamily (set at IdCard.js:115, 132, 140, 159), so the card text renders in Open Sans and the browser does download the woff2 on that public page. The premise "Nothing on a public or article page references it" is disproven.

(2) MEASURED IMPACT IS ZERO FOR SEARCH. I fetched both real Google Fonts responses. Both families: 19,441 bytes raw / 1,861 gzipped / 41 @font-face blocks. Inter alone: 7,413 raw / 699 gzipped / 21 blocks. The delta is ~1.16 KB gzipped. The full current response at 1.86 KB gzipped fits far inside the ~14 KB initial congestion window, so it arrives in the same single round trip with or without Open Sans. Dropping the family removes zero HTTP requests and zero round trips; the same one `<link>` to fonts.googleapis.com is still issued and still render-blocking. FCP/LCP delta is unmeasurable, and Google's page experience signal reads field Core Web Vitals, which a sub-2 KB change to an already-fetched stylesheet cannot move.

(3) THE PROPOSED FIX IS HARMFUL. "Simply change cardLayout.js:25 to 'Gilroy', sans-serif" would silently regress every browser ID-card preview. Gilroy is registered ONLY server-side for @react-pdf at `IdCardDocument.js:7-13` via `Font.register` pointing at local .ttf paths. There is no `@font-face` for Gilroy in any stylesheet (grep for `@font-face` across `css/` returns nothing; grep for "Gilroy" outside node_modules hits only cardLayout.js and IdCardDocument.js). In a browser 'Gilroy' resolves to nothing and text falls back to generic sans-serif.

NO MITIGATION EXISTS, but none is needed: there is no `next/font` usage and no `optimizeFonts` in `next.config.js`, so the link genuinely stays render-blocking. It blocks identically either way, which is precisely why removing the second family buys nothing.

At most this is non-SEO code hygiene, and even that is weak since the family is actually consumed. The one real adjacent perf gap is different and not what was reported: `app/layout.js:54` preconnects to `fonts.gstatic.com` but never to `fonts.googleapis.com`, the origin serving the render-blocking stylesheet.

title: SVG and file-loader rules exist only in the webpack branch while `turbopack: {}` is declared and the build is pinned to --webpack
why:
The quoted code is genuine, but the finding does not describe an SEO defect, and its central causal claim is factually wrong.

1. Evidence accurate, line range off by one. next.config.js:27 is `turbopack: {},`. The webpack block spans :30-50, not :30-49 (`return config` is line 49, `},` closes at line 50). The two rules are :31-42 (file-loader) and :44-47 (@svgr/webpack). package.json pins `--webpack` on :7 (dev), :8 (build), and also :10 (analyze), which the finding missed. The ten .svg imports exist at components/social-icons/index.js:1-8 and components/Icon.js:1-2, and Footer.js:10-15 renders six of them. A grep for static `png|jpe?g|gif|mp4` imports across app/ components/ layouts/ pages/ lib/ returns zero hits, and there are zero CSS `url()` image references, so the file-loader rule is inert as claimed.

2. No live effect, by the finding's own admission ("No live effect while --webpack is present"). The mitigation already sits in the repo: every build entry point carries the flag. Nothing today is slower, broken, or unindexable.

3. The "silently removes" premise is wrong. Drop the flag and Turbopack resolves `import Mail from './mail.svg'` to a StaticImageData object. Icon.js:14 renders `<IconSvg className={...} />`, passing a plain object as a React element type, which throws "Element type is invalid". Footer sits inside LayoutWrapper.js:85, so every prerendered route fails during `next build`. A build that fails never deploys. That is the loudest possible failure, the opposite of silent, and it can never reach a crawler.

4. The CLS branch is doubly hypothetical and self-cancelling. It needs the flag to STAY (so file-loader stays live) AND someone to add a static image import that does not exist. All current image use goes through next/image with runtime path strings or the `remotePatterns` allowlist at next.config.js:56-68, none of which touch a webpack loader.

5. Bundler choice is not a search-engine signal. Webpack and Turbopack emit equivalent production output on Next 16.2.3. Turbopack's advantage is compile speed, a developer-experience gain that never reaches a crawler or a visitor's Core Web Vitals. `turbopack: {}` is an inert no-op key, not a mode switch, so the "false impression" point is config cosmetics.

This is a build-maintainability note, not an SEO audit item. It does not hurt organic search for the blog articles in any measurable way.

title: The only path to 72 of 77 articles is a Previous/Next-only pager 16 clicks deep
why:
The code quotes are accurate, but the load-bearing claim in the title and impact ("the ONLY path", "no sitemap backstop", critical) is false. Two full-coverage discovery paths exist in the repo that the finding never examined.

WHAT VERIFIED AS CLAIMED: components/Pagination.js:16 and :29 are quoted correctly and emit only Previous/Next. app/blog/page.js:11 and app/blog/page/[page]/page.js:6 both set POSTS_PER_PAGE = 5. components/Footer.js has no /blog link. layouts/ListLayout.js:58 gates the pager on `pagination`. The rel=prev/next reasoning is correct, not folklore: Google dropped it as an indexing signal in 2019, and the finding rightly declines to recommend it. The deployed sitemap really will be near-empty (public/tags/ is untracked, `git ls-files public/tags` returns 0, mtimes are 2026-02-12, and nothing in the codebase writes it, so the local 63-URL public/sitemap.xml is a stale artifact) — but that is the already-established sitemap fact being double-counted here, not IA evidence.

REFUTATION 1, /feed.xml is a complete discovery backstop. app/feed.xml/route.js:22 calls `listArticles({ includeDrafts: false, pageSize: 9999 })` and line 11 emits `<link>${siteMetadata.siteUrl}/blog/${post.slug}</link>` for every published article. app/layout.js:53 serves `<link rel="alternate" type="application/rss+xml" href="/feed.xml" />` on every page. Google supports RSS 2.0 as a sitemap format and crawls autodiscovered feeds. A flat, hourly-revalidated list of all 77 article URLs sits one hop from the home page. "Sequential Next-clicking is Googlebot's only discovery route" and "no sitemap backstop" are both false.

REFUTATION 2, the finding inverted its own tag-page evidence. It cited app/tags/[tag]/page.js:55 as a defect because no `pagination` is passed. But that line is `<ListLayout posts={filteredPosts} title={title} />` — it also passes no `initialDisplayPosts`, so layouts/ListLayout.js:7 defaults it to `[]` and lines 15-16 fall through to `displayPosts = filteredBlogPosts`. Tag pages therefore render EVERY article carrying that tag, unpaginated, each as a real anchor via components/articles/ArticleItem.js:32. Tag pages are flat complete indexes, the opposite of what was concluded. I ran a BFS over the 62 stale tag feeds: the largest tag-connected component reaches 28 of 63 articles, so roughly 44% of the corpus sits 3 clicks from home (home -> /blog -> /tags/X -> article), not 12-16.

SEVERITY: critical means "cannot rank or are not indexable at all." Articles are indexable — no noindex anywhere (app/layout.js:30 robots block and components/SEO.js:10 `content="follow, index"` are the only robots directives), and app/blog/[...slug]/page.js:10-15 statically pre-renders all of them. This is a crawl-efficiency and internal-linking weakness, not an indexability blocker. Medium.

RESIDUAL ISSUE WORTH KEEPING (narrower than claimed): the /tags index is orphaned. app/tags/page.js:49 links all 62 tags in one page, which would put every article at depth 3, but grepping for links to "/tags" across app/, components/, data/, layouts/, pages/ returns only revalidatePath() calls in app/api/admin/*. No nav or footer entry exists. Adding /tags to data/headerNavLinks.js is a one-line fix worth more than rewriting the pager.

title: The events page contains no events, no dates, no locations and no Event schema
why:
The quotes are accurate, but the finding is a product feature request, not an SEO defect, and its severity is inflated by two levels.

1. NOT AN SEO PROBLEM IN THE CODE. No event data exists anywhere: not in the repo, not in S3, not in Sheets. A grep across lib/, data/, and app/api/ returns only an external form URL at data/siteMetadata.js:31 (`event: 'https://my.forms.app/form/6205262c015f7839d8439ca9'`). The proposed fix requires inventing content that does not exist. An SEO audit finds defects in how EXISTING content reaches search engines. "Publish an event calendar" is content strategy and product roadmap.

2. THE FIX CONTRADICTS A STATED BUSINESS DECISION THE FINDING ITSELF QUOTES. app/events/page.js:43-45 says the agenda is full and the request channel is closed on purpose. The finding cites this text as damage, then recommends the organization chase more inbound event demand.

3. EVENT JSON-LD CANNOT LEGITIMATELY BE ADDED. Google requires Event structured data to describe an event that is visible on the page. With zero events, adding `Event` markup is a structured-data policy violation and risks a manual action, not a rich result. The recommendation is technically unsound as written.

4. IMPACT IS PURE SPECULATION, WHICH THE AUDIT GROUND RULES FORBID. "Competitors and Facebook capture this traffic" cites no keyword data, no analytics, and no ranking data. No file:line supports it.

5. WRONG PRIORITY. The audit instructs prioritizing findings that hurt organic search for the blog ARTICLES. This finding has zero effect on article indexing, crawling, or ranking.

6. EVIDENCE IMPRECISION. The claim "the only JSON-LD on the site is the per-article Article at app/blog/[...slug]/page.js:103-104" is wrong. components/SEO.js:104-105 also emits `'@context': 'https://schema.org'` / `'@type': 'Article'`.

7. THE DISCOVERABILITY PREMISE BELONGS TO A DIFFERENT DEFECT. /events is absent from public/sitemap.xml because scripts/generate-sitemap.js:9-15 globs only `pages/*.js`, `data/blog/**`, and `public/tags/**`. App Router routes are never enumerated. That is the already-known sitemap finding, not this one.

8. NO RANKING LOSS EXISTS. Nothing regressed. Content was never created. "High = major ranking/CTR loss" does not apply to a page that never held the rankings.

The only salvageable kernel is thin: /events carries no geographic text, and the site has no Organization or LocalBusiness schema at all. That is a minor on-page polish item worth at most low severity, and the "keyword must appear in the h1" reasoning behind it leans on weak, dated on-page advice. Modern ranking uses entity and location signals, not literal h1 keyword matching.

title: Articles link only to the chronological neighbour, so the 16 comet articles never link to each other
why: The finding's line citations are accurate, but its central claim is factually wrong: a hub-and-spoke topic cluster already exists. The tag chips at BlogPost.js:108-112 are not decoration - components/Tag.js:6-9 renders each as `<Link href={`/tags/${kebabCase(text)}`}>`. The hub at app/tags/[tag]/page.js:45-48 loads every published article with `pageSize: 9999` and filters by kebab-cased tag with no cap, then line 55 renders `<ListLayout posts={filteredPosts} title={title} />` with no `initialDisplayPosts` and no `pagination` prop, so ListLayout.js:15-16 falls through to `filteredBlogPosts` and prints ALL matching articles. Each one emits real server-rendered anchors via components/articles/ArticleItem.js:11, 32 and 45 (`<Link href={`/blog/${slug}`}>`). So every comet article links to /tags/cometa, and /tags/cometa links back to all 16. That is the standard, recommended topic-cluster pattern, not an absence of one. The hubs are also indexable and discoverable: app/layout.js:30-40 sets `robots: { index: true, follow: true }` with no override in app/tags/[tag]/page.js's generateMetadata (lines 27-39, which sets only title/description/alternates), public/tags/ contains 62 tag directories including cometa, meteoro and asteroide, and public/sitemap.xml contains 62 `/tags/*` <loc> entries. The claims "form no topic cluster", "Internal PageRank cannot flow", and "Google gets no same-topic link signal" are therefore all refuted by code the author did not grep for. Separately, the supporting stat "only 2 in-body internal links across all 77 articles" cannot be verified from this repo at all: data/blog is empty and article bodies live in S3, so that number is unverifiable evidence. What survives is a much smaller point: cluster siblings are 2 hops apart (article -> tag hub -> sibling) instead of 1, and a direct "Articulos relacionados" block would shorten that. That is an incremental polish item on top of a working structure, not a high-severity ranking defect, so severity is downgraded from high to low.

title: 39 of 61 tag pages list exactly one article and every one is index,follow
why: Evidence quotes are genuine but the SEO reasoning fails on four counts. (1) The load-bearing impact claim, crawl-budget dilution, is folklore at this scale. Google's documented position is that crawl budget is not a concern below roughly a few thousand URLs. This site totals under ~200 URLs (77 articles + 62 tag slugs + ~16 /blog/page/N + a handful of static routes), so 39 thin tag pages cannot starve 77 articles of crawl. (2) The secondary claim that a cluster of thin listings is a site-quality negative has no documented mechanism for a small legitimate blog. Google's normal handling of a one-item tag archive is to crawl it and decline to index it, a self-correcting default. Each tag page also has a distinct H1 and a distinct filtered result set, so it is not duplicate content in the canonical sense. (3) The proposed fix is net-harmful on this specific site. app/blog/page.js:11 sets POSTS_PER_PAGE = 5 and the sitemap contains zero article URLs, so tag pages are a live crawl path into deep articles. Removing thin tags from generateStaticParams and from the /tags index, as proposed, would delete internal links to exactly the articles the audit aims to help. (4) Root cause is misattributed. scripts/generate-sitemap.js:8-15 globs 'public/tags/**/*.xml' alongside an empty 'data/blog/**', so the tag-only sitemap composition is a symptom of the already-known sitemap bug, not a deliberate tag-indexing strategy. Fixing that bug resolves the prioritization signal without touching tags. Counts are also slightly off and not independently reproducible: recounting from the committed per-tag feeds gives 62 slugs with 40 single-article, not 61 with 39.

title: Seven singular/plural and synonym tag pairs split the topic clusters into thin duplicate pages
why:
The raw counts are real, but the interpretation is wrong on 4 of the 7 pairs, and the proposed fix would damage the taxonomy.

VERIFIED AS ACCURATE: kebabCase.js is quoted correctly (lib/utils/kebabCase.js:3 = `const kebabCase = (str) => slug(str)`, plain github-slugger, no alias layer). All 14 slugs exist as prerendered pages and as sitemap entries. I recounted every page from the build output (counting the ArticleItem wrapper, not raw /blog/ hrefs, because headerNavLinks.js:11 puts `/blog/telescopios` on every page) and got the claimed numbers exactly: meteoro 10, meteoros 1, meteorito 2, luna 4, lunas 3, telescopio 1, telescopios 1, jwst 2, james-webb 2, swan 1, c2025-r2-swan 1, 67p 1, churyumov-gerasimenko 1, cometa 16, cometa-oscuro 1.

REFUTATION 1 - four pairs are not duplicates, they are distinct topics.
| Claimed pair | What the pages actually hold | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| swan / c2025-r2-swan | swan = comet C/2025 F2 SWAN. c2025-r2-swan = comet C/2025 R2 SWAN in a seven-comet roundup. | Two DIFFERENT comets. "The same comet" is factually false. |
| luna / lunas | luna = 4 lunar-eclipse articles on Earth's Moon. lunas = Enceladus, Saturn 20, new moons of Saturn. | Different subjects. Merging is wrong. |
| meteoro / meteorito | meteorito = a New Jersey meteorite and a PR impact crater. | Distinct astronomical concepts in Spanish (light phenomenon vs recovered rock). Merging degrades precision. |
| cometa / cometa-oscuro | The one cometa-oscuro article, /blog/2024/10/30/Cometa_Oscuro_1998_KY26, is ALSO on /tags/cometa. | Not a split at all. Broad tag plus narrow sub-tag. Correct taxonomy. |

The same broad-plus-narrow pattern also holds for 67p (Cometa67P is on /tags/cometa) and both SWAN tags, so no cluster is actually orphaned from the main comet hub. The claim "14 URLs where 7 should exist" is wrong. The defensible number is 6 URLs where 3 should exist.

REFUTATION 2 - half the proposed fix already exists. The admin editor already autocompletes from the existing tag set, so authors are already steered to reuse tags.

REFUTATION 3 - SEO reasoning is inflated. The pairs are thin, not duplicate: /tags/meteoro (10 articles) and /tags/meteoros (1 article) serve different content, so no duplicate-content problem exists there. Only jwst/james-webb and 67p/churyumov-gerasimenko are true near-duplicates. Google resolves such pairs by picking one and dropping the other, which costs crawl budget, not rankings. The claim that a merged 13-article archive "could plausibly rank for 'meteoro Puerto Rico'" is speculation. Google surfaces the article, not the tag archive, for that query shape, and 1-to-2-item archives are routinely left unindexed. The far larger defect in the same area is that public/sitemap.xml submits 62 tag URLs and zero article URLs, so tag hygiene is a second-order concern behind that.

RESIDUAL, at low severity: two genuine duplicate pairs (jwst/james-webb, 67p/churyumov-gerasimenko) and one genuine plural pair (meteoro/meteoros). These are content-hygiene items to fix in S3 tag data, not through a code-level alias map.

title: Accented tags produce percent-encoded URLs, inconsistent with article slugs
why:
The code mechanism is real, but the evidence is partly false and the SEO impact is not. Three problems.

1. Fabricated evidence. The finding states both encoded URLs "are in the committed public/sitemap.xml". public/sitemap.xml is NOT committed. .gitignore:14 lists "public/sitemap.xml" and .gitignore:19 lists "*.xml"; `git ls-files public/sitemap.xml` returns nothing and `git ls-files public/tags` returns 0 files. The sitemap and the public/tags/*/feed.xml files are untracked local build artifacts on the auditor machine, not repository content.

2. Unverifiable counts, and no production crawl surface. The claimed "1 article" and "2 articles" come from those stale local feed.xml files dated Feb 2026. No script in the repo generates public/tags feeds any more (only app/feed.xml/route.js and lib/generate-rss.js exist; there is no app/tags/[tag]/feed.xml route). Articles live in S3, so live tag values cannot be confirmed from the repo. Further, scripts/generate-sitemap.js:12 globs 'public/tags/**/*.xml', a gitignored path, so on a clean Vercel checkout it matches nothing and the deployed sitemap contains zero tag URLs. The claimed sitemap exposure does not exist in production.

3. Obsolete SEO advice. Google indexes percent-encoded UTF-8 URL paths normally and decodes them for display in search results. "Ugly in SERPs" is not current search-engine behavior. URL cosmetics are not a ranking signal. The duplicate-page argument is conditional on a future author typo, and it is not distinctive: the taxonomy already fragments on plain word variants with no accents involved (/tags/luna, /tags/lunar, /tags/lunas, /tags/meteoro, /tags/meteoros). Article slugs are already accent free through lib/articles.js:67, so blog articles, the stated audit priority, take no harm at all.

What survives is a code-consistency nit on two thin tag listing pages, not an SEO defect. Severity drops from medium to low.

title: The site-wide footer links to nothing but the home page
why:
The literal code quote is accurate, but the SEO claim it rests on is false, and the proposed fix is nearly all duplication.

1. Evidence check. components/Footer.js is correct as quoted. Lines 10-15 render six SocialIcons. Lines 20-22 render author and copyright year. Line 25 is `<Link href="/" className="block text-center sm:inline sm:text-left">`, the only internal link. components/LayoutWrapper.js:84-86 renders `<SectionContainer><Footer /></SectionContainer>`. app/layout.js:53 is `<link rel="alternate" type="application/rss+xml" href="/feed.xml" />`, and app/feed.xml/route.js exists. One factual error: data/headerNavLinks.js carries 11 active links, not 12. Line 10 comments out `/gallery`.

2. Decisive mitigation. The IMPACT claim says a footer hub "is the cheapest way to make /blog, /tags, /guides and /events reachable in one click from every article." Those pages are already one click from every article. The SAME component that renders the Footer also renders the header nav. components/LayoutWrapper.js:67-71 renders `NavigationLinks`, which maps all 11 headerNavLinks at lines 102-110 and 112-121. components/LayoutWrapper.js:65 renders `MobileNav`, which maps all 11 links again at components/MobileNav.js:62-72. Both are in the server-rendered HTML. `NavigationLinks` is only CSS-hidden by `hidden xl:flex`, and MobileNav is moved off-canvas by `translate-x-full`, not removed. app/blog/[...slug]/page.js:130 wraps every article in `<LayoutWrapper>` with no forceLightHeader, so the full nav ships on every article.

3. Further mitigation inside the article template. layouts/PostLayout.js:133-139 renders `<Link href="/blog">← Volver</Link>` in the article body on every post. layouts/PostLayout.js:100-105 renders `<Tag>` chips, and components/Tag.js:7 points them at `/tags/${kebabCase(text)}`. layouts/PostLayout.js:116 and :126 render prev and next article links.

Proposed footer link vs. actual existing coverage:
- /blog: already in headerNavLinks.js:8 and PostLayout.js:135
- /guides: already headerNavLinks.js:9
- /blog/telescopios: already headerNavLinks.js:11
- /about, /contact, /events, /membership, /donate: already headerNavLinks.js:2-7
- /weather, /brand: already headerNavLinks.js:4 and :12
- /feed.xml: already app/layout.js:53
- /tags/[tag]: already components/Tag.js:7 on every article
- /tags index and /links: genuinely unlinked, the only new items

4. The pagination rationale is a non-sequitur. app/blog/page.js:11 sets POSTS_PER_PAGE = 5, and components/Pagination.js:16 and :29 chain one page at a time. A footer link to /blog does nothing for the depth of /blog/page/12, because /blog is page 1 and the header already links it. Article prev/next links at PostLayout.js:116 and :126 already chain every article independent of pagination.

5. The premise is weak SEO. Search engines discount repeated boilerplate navigation. A second copy of links that already sit in the site-wide header adds no discovery path and no meaningful equity, since the first link to a URL on a page is what carries anchor text weight.

Residual truth is small. Only /tags (app/tags/page.js) is a genuinely orphaned index. Nothing links to it. app/links/page.js is a bio-link page forced to light theme at app/providers.js:15 and is not a search target. That residue is a low-severity orphan-page note, not "the footer links to nothing but the home page" at medium severity.

title: Five public routes are linked from nowhere, including the tag index and the site's only sitemap entry
why:
The finding's two load-bearing claims are false or already mitigated, and it has no bearing on article ranking.

1. Claim (d) is factually WRONG. The finding says /gallery "is the one and only URL the deployed sitemap emits" and calls the sitemap situation "inverted". The committed public/sitemap.xml contains 63 <loc> entries: one /gallery and 62 /tags/<tag> URLs. The glob at scripts/generate-sitemap.js:12 is 'public/tags/**/*.xml', and public/tags/ holds 62 directories each with a feed.xml; the path rewrite at generate-sitemap.js:23 and :29 turns public/tags/cometa/feed.xml into /tags/cometa. A regenerated sitemap produces the same set. The narrative that Google is told about exactly one orphaned hidden page is not true.

2. The sub-claim the finding calls "the costliest" is ALREADY HANDLED. It argues /tags is the hub that "would flatten the topic clusters and shorten the path to older articles". That hub already exists in distributed form: components/Tag.js:6-7 renders a Link to /tags/<kebab> and is rendered on every article card (components/articles/ArticleItem.js:38), every article page (app/blog/[...slug]/BlogPost.js:110, layouts/PostLayout.js:103), so all 62 tag pages are internally linked from the blog listing and from each post. app/tags/[tag]/page.js:55 then renders ListLayout over every matching article, linking each /blog/<slug>. The same 62 tag pages are also in the sitemap. The /tags index is a hub-of-hubs whose children are already linked and crawled. Its absence from data/headerNavLinks.js costs close to nothing.

3. Three of the five routes cannot lose equity because they can never be discovered. /links, /media/<slug> and /card-test-longname are orphaned AND absent from public/sitemap.xml AND have no external inbound link. A URL Google never discovers accumulates no equity and loses none. That is code hygiene, not an SEO defect. /links is orphaned deliberately, not accidentally: app/providers.js:14-15 comments "Force light theme for /links page (social links page)", i.e. a bio-link landing page entered from social profiles. app/card-test-longname/page.js:1 is 'use client' and renders an ID-card image with no indexable prose. The `revalidatePath('/media')` on a non-existent route (app/api/admin/media/route.js:149) is a dead call, not a search issue.

4. It does not touch the stated priority. Blog articles are reachable through /blog (app/blog/page.js), /blog/page/N (components/Pagination.js:16,29) and 62 tag pages. None of the five orphan routes sits on an article's crawl path.

Residual truth: /tags, /links and /card-test-longname are genuinely unlinked, and app/card-test-longname/page.js:9 does say "Delete this directory once review is done." That is low-severity cleanup, not a medium ranking problem, and the finding's own justification for medium rests on a false sitemap claim.

title: The home page renders no H1 at all
why:
REFUTED on its central factual claim. The title and the evidence both assert the home page "renders no H1 at all" and that "its first content element" is the description paragraph. That is wrong. app/HomeContent.js:41-63 mounts three ImageWidget instances and app/HomeContent.js:64 mounts an ApodWidget, and each of those components emits an `<h1>` (components/widgets/ImageWidget.js:22, components/widgets/ApodWidget.js:5). The home page therefore renders three H1s in the server HTML plus a fourth once APOD loads. The reporting agent never opened the widget components it was citing through, so the claim that no H1 exists, the claim that the outline "jumps straight to H2s", and the claim of a clean document outline elsewhere are all unverified by the reporter and contradicted by the code.

The impact claim also rests on obsolete weighting. Google has repeatedly stated H1 is a minor signal, that zero H1s and multiple H1s are both handled, and that it uses whatever headings and text it finds. Saying the home page "has no way to claim 'Sociedad de Astronomía del Caribe' as its topic" is not defensible when app/layout.js:9-12 sets that exact string as the `<title>`, app/layout.js:14-22 repeats it in OpenGraph, components/LayoutWrapper.js:36 puts it in an aria-label on the home link, components/Footer.js:25-27 puts it in visible anchor text, and app/HomeContent.js:22-24 renders the full Spanish description server-side. The topical signal is present through the strongest channel available.

A genuine but different and smaller issue does exist: the two widget components use `<h1>` for decorative widget captions, which is a semantic/accessibility defect and leaves the home page without a heading that names the organization. That is worth a low-severity cleanup (demote the widget headings to h2/h3, then optionally add one real H1). It is not the finding as written, it is not medium, and the ground rules explicitly bar reporting a problem whose cited code was not checked. The finding should be rejected and re-filed against the widget components if the parent wants it tracked. The home page is fully indexable and ranks on title, description, and body copy regardless.

title: 404 responses carry no header, no footer and no internal links
why:
Refuted on three independent grounds.

1. A load-bearing claim is factually false. The finding states "Neither renders LayoutWrapper." That is wrong for pages/404.js. pages/_app.js:30 wraps EVERY Pages Router page, 404.js included, in `<LayoutWrapper forceLightHeader={router.pathname === '/links'}>`. LayoutWrapper.js:69 renders `<NavigationLinks />` (the full headerNavLinks set) and LayoutWrapper.js:85 renders `<Footer />`. So pages/404.js, if it rendered at all, would carry the nav and footer, not "at most one link out."

2. The pages/404.js half of the finding is moot: that file is unreachable for unmatched URLs in this hybrid app. node_modules/next/dist/server/base-server.js:1682-1696 resolves 404s by first trying the app-dir `UNDERSCORE_NOT_FOUND_ROUTE_ENTRY` when `hasAppDir` is true, and only falls back to `/404` when that returns null. Next always emits that entry: the existing build's .next/app-path-routes-manifest.json contains `"/_not-found/page": "/_not-found"` even though no app/not-found.js exists. The English copy at pages/404.js:13-15 is therefore dead code, and the proposed "localise pages/404.js" fix would change nothing a user or crawler ever sees.

3. The SEO impact rests on folklore. 404 responses carry HTTP 404 plus, for `notFound()` paths, an injected `<meta name="robots" content="noindex" />` (documented in node_modules/next/dist/client/components/not-found.js, the notFound() docblock; called at app/blog/[...slug]/page.js:66 and :71). Google drops such URLs rather than crawling onward from them, and links on a non-indexable 404 page carry no ranking signal, so "every dead end matters" does not hold. The genuine SEO failure mode here would be a soft 404 (HTTP 200 with not-found content), and this repo does not have one: the blog catch-all returns a true 404 for missing articles and for `article.draft`.

What remains is real but non-SEO: the app-router 404 is Next's built-in English page rendered inside app/layout.js:43-66, which mounts only `<Providers>{children}</Providers>` and no site chrome. That is a UX and localization polish item on an es-PR site, not an organic-search problem, and it does not belong in an SEO audit ranked against the blog-article findings.

title: On-site search is a client-side filter with no URL, no server route and no full-text coverage
why:
The code quote is genuine, but the finding is not an SEO problem, one impact sub-claim is factually wrong, and the proposed fix contradicts current Google guidance.

| Claim | Verdict |
| --- | --- |
| ListLayout.js:8-16 is the whole search implementation | CONFIRMED, quoted verbatim, line numbers exact |
| Never touches article bodies | CONFIRMED, and structural: `content` is in ARTICLE_FIELDS (lib/articles.js:15) but omitted from INDEX_FIELDS (lib/articles.js:25-38), and listArticles reads only the index (lib/articles.js:182) |
| Produces no URL | CONFIRMED, no useSearchParams and no router.push in layouts/ListLayout.js |
| No /search route in app/ or pages/ | CONFIRMED, only app/api/admin/catalog/search, an admin API |
| Users get matching "over one page's data" | FALSE, see below |
| SEO impact | NONE, self-admitted "not a direct ranking factor" |

1. The "one page's data" impact is wrong. app/blog/page.js:25 and app/blog/page/[page]/page.js:42 both call `listArticles({ includeDrafts: false, pageSize: 9999 })` under the comment "Get ALL published articles for client-side search", then pass `posts={allResult.articles}` (page.js:35, [page]/page.js:52). The filter runs over the entire published corpus, not one page. The stated user harm does not occur.

2. Internal site search is not a ranking signal. Googlebot does not type into the input and does not run the filter. It is orthogonal to indexing.

3. Article crawlability, the only real SEO concern in this area, is already handled elsewhere. components/Pagination.js:16 and :29 render real `Link` hrefs to `/blog/` and `/blog/page/N`, and app/blog/page/[page]/page.js:13-22 pre-renders every page number via generateStaticParams. Crawlers reach every article without the search box.

4. The proposed fix is obsolete advice inverted. Google documents internal search result pages as crawl traps and thin near-duplicate content, and advises keeping them out of the index. Adding a crawlable `/search?q=` route is a net SEO negative unless noindexed, so the fix would create the problem it claims to solve.

Residual value is UX only, which the brief excludes. Not reportable in an SEO audit.
